1	# Working discipline
2	
3	- **Starting any requested change** — begin from the *problem*, not the solution, in any
4	  repository and not just this one. Reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the
5	  problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way
6	  to solve it; a different fix, or none, may serve better.
7	
8	- **Replying to an owner comment** — open with an explicit classification line,
9	  `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other`, where `other` covers questions,
10	  approvals and command phrases and a mixed comment names each part. An automation dispatch prompt
11	  is a comment too: class `other`, in your *first* substantive reply rather than at the end of the
12	  run. Put the class **alone on the line** and any explanation on the next one: the line is scanned
13	  for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu declares all of them. A class cannot be taken
14	  back, and a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first.
15	
16	- **Acting on a correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then
17	  rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands,
18	  but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
19	
20	- **Acting on a feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements
21	  document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it
22	  fail, then implement until it passes.
23	
24	- **Acting on a process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. Land it as durable
25	  rules in the project's local scope, its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs), routed
26	  through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → schema → hook → check → skill
27	  → prose). Promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not
28	  the interactive session's.
29	
30	- **Choosing what goes on that ladder** — only a rule that constrains *how work is done* and
31	  outlives any one feature; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place. Reject two shapes
32	  outright: a check that asserts particular code exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a
33	  point in time), and a rule derivable from the product's requirements (that is a requirement —
34	  take it to the feature path, the requirements document and the test that proves it).
35	
36	- **Landing a rule anywhere on the ladder** — author the assurance first, the check the future
37	  world must satisfy, execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green.
38	  At the prose rung, where no check can carry an in-flight judgment rule, the equivalent step is
39	  showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.
40	
41	- **Building a mechanism for a behavior** — verify against a real run that it isn't already
42	  provided.
43	
44	- **Building release, deploy, versioning or CI plumbing** — look for the shared pack that owns it
45	  first; copying a mechanic from a sibling repo is the tell that it belongs centrally. If no pack
46	  owns it, report the gap rather than author a third copy.
47	
48	- **Finishing a change** — watch it work **now**; never park it on "check tomorrow". What a task
49	  costs is its shelf-life, the time from starting it until everyone can forget about it.
50	
51	- **Changing scheduled or unattended machinery** — force a run now (the scheduler's wake lever, a
52	  `workflow_dispatch`, the fleet-wide force sweep) and watch it to a terminal state rather than wait
53	  for its next natural run.
54	
55	- **Planning a migration** — prefer the design that converges in one forced pass to the one that
56	  trickles across nightly cycles, accept legacy input at the door so nothing has to wait for
57	  stragglers, and drive the stragglers with a standing mechanism rather than a phase someone must
58	  remember to close. Write every phase's code — the cleanup, the destructive tail and every
59	  legacy tolerance's removal included — before asking for approval, and chain each execution step
60	  to the verification of the one before it rather than to anyone's memory;
61	  [writing-migration-plans](skills/writing-migration-plans/SKILL.md) owns that ordering and the
62	  chain's mechanics.
63	
64	- **Adding a legacy tolerance** (a dual read, an accepted old spelling, a shim) — it is
65	  scaffolding, not a feature: ship it with an advisory that fires where the old shape is still in
66	  use, and with its removal already a link in the migration's chain, due one stated convergence
67	  window after that advisory reaches the holders. (2)
68	
69	- **Choosing an automerge policy for a PR or a chain link** — write it as a prediction of the
70	  change's shape, the folders and kinds you expect the diff to touch, and never widen it to fit the
71	  diff that arrived: a policy that fails is the speed bump that puts a person back on the trail,
72	  not an error to route around. (1)
73	
74	- **Predicting a change that could delete production data or degrade the experience past what a
75	  later PR undoes** — its policy is `nothing`, whatever its diff class; irreversibility is the
76	  first of the two things review here exists to catch. (1)
77	
78	- **Handing over a change whose diff reached more folders or files than its request implied** —
79	  say so, and name the abstraction that would have kept it in one place: the reviewer reads which
80	  folders moved to judge whether the change made sense, and a wide diff for a small ask is the
81	  growth lesson review is for, not a defect. (1)
82	
83	- **When verifying now is genuinely impossible** (an external release window, an upstream fix in
84	  flight, an effect that only appears once the change is deployed, converged or loaded by a later
85	  session) — the follow-up is a mechanism that comes to you, never a human's memory and never an
86	  offer to the owner to go and check later. File it with
87	  [verify-in-production](skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md), unasked, **once the PR has
88	  merged** and never before — a PR can be rejected, and a still-open branch can be rewritten
89	  under you, either of which strands a verification whose premise never reached `main`. The
90	  skill owns both halves — whether this change needs one at all (most don't; a test that ran is
91	  already the mechanism), and the issue that states what puts the change in production and what
92	  proves it works there.
93	
94	- **Finishing a larger element** — one that earned a design doc or a phased tracking issue — a
95	  point verification is not enough: schedule the review that comes back once the element has
96	  lived in production about a week, asking whether it is working, misused, overused or underused
97	  against its real record — with the brief written at design time, expected amounts, signals and
98	  the metrics that measure them included, never improvised when the review runs.
99	  [production-retrospective](skills/production-retrospective/SKILL.md) owns the trigger, the
100	  brief, and the lane's other classes — canon, local-pack and fleet alike.
101	
102	- **Receiving feedback that flags a misunderstanding** — check whether the artifact is already
103	  correct before expanding it; if it is, say so and push back rather than edit.
104	
105	- **Writing anything** — size it to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three
106	  paragraphs.
107	
108	- **Correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source** — derive the corrected
109	  version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to
110	  surface what was actually wrong.
111	
112	- **Acting on an approval to merge, ship or proceed** — it applies only *backward*, to the work
113	  already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A
114	  later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval — and a
115	  multiple-choice answer is not an approval at all, even when an option's wording mentioned the
116	  action.
117	
118	## Harness-tool contracts
119	
120	- **Searching for a tool with `ToolSearch`** — a search that finds nothing is evidence about your
121	  query, not about the environment. Search the fully-qualified name (`select:mcp__<server>__<tool>`,
122	  copied off the deferred-tools listing) and try the tool before telling the owner a step is theirs;
123	  the bare short name returns "no matching tools", which reads exactly like absence.
124	
125	- **Calling `Edit`** — the file must have been read *with the read tool*; `cat`/`grep`/`sed` don't
126	  count. The moment shell output tells you which file you're about to change, read that exact path;
127	  a narrow offset window satisfies it.
128	
129	- **Calling `Grep` with a context flag** (`-n`/`-A`/`-B`/`-C`) — it's silently ignored under the
130	  default `output_mode: "files_with_matches"`, so the call answers only a match count or file
131	  list, never the lines you asked for, with no error to catch it. Pass `output_mode: "content"`
132	  in the same call as any context flag.
133	
134	- **Scheduling a wake-up with the harness** — pass `prompt`, the instruction the woken turn is to
135	  act on, on any call that isn't `stop: true`; a no-op flag and a stated `reason` do not exempt it,
136	  and the call is rejected without it. A rejection leaves no fallback armed, which is what the
137	  `unattended-agents` skill's re-issue rule is for.
138	
139	## Warnings and findings
140	
141	- **Seeing a build, test or CI warning** — fix it rather than tolerate it, with a small, targeted
142	  fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change.
143	
144	- **Suppressing a warning** — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`,
145	  swallowing it — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path. Reach for it only as a
146	  deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected, and **carry the
147	  reason at the site**, on the suppression line or the comment immediately above it; that inline
148	  reason *is* the review record, so record no second justification elsewhere.
149	
150	- **Waiving a finding on *text* rather than code** — try deleting the flagged phrase first; a
151	  waiver is for a crossing that genuinely must exist.
152	
153	- **Working around a finding from a vendored check** — confirm the vendored copy is current first;
154	  the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in.
155	
156	- **Deferring a warning you can't fix now with a small cause-addressing change** (it waits on an
157	  upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor) — open a dedicated issue unless one is
158	  already open, then move on. Search for that open one by the **invariant identifier** the finding
159	  names — the symbol, path or id it is *about* — never the sentence it arrived in: every filer
160	  paraphrases the message and prefixes its own stage's name, so the wording is the one part that
161	  differs across filings, and a new branch, PR number or run is not a new finding. Resolving it, by
162	  real fix or a consciously-chosen suppression, happens in that issue's own change.
163	
164	# The task lifecycle
165	
166	For every new task:
167	
168	1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
169	2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`,
170	   `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
171	3. Open the PR with a closing keyword for that issue on its own line in the **body** —
172	   `Closes #123`. That is what fills GitHub's *Development* panel, the link between PR and issue
173	   that anyone browsing either one follows; `Refs #123` is a cross-reference and links nothing
174	   there. A PR that must not close its issue — one slice of a longer plan, one of several against
175	   a tracker — still links: give the slice its own issue and close that one.
176	4. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.
177	
178	- **Spotting a change that should wait until the work in flight lands** — file it as work that
179	  comes back on its own rather than doing it now or trusting anyone to remember it: the
180	  [do-later](skills/do-later/SKILL.md) skill, which queues it behind what it waits on.
181	
182	- **Filing anything into the ad-hoc queue** (a deferral, a verification, any marked issue) — it
183	  asks an unattended session **on this repository** to do the work, so only file what such a
184	  session can actually do here. A read of another repository or a console is not work it can
185	  do: that item parks minutes after it is picked, and a park is a person's problem filed under
186	  a mechanism's name. A public URL is the one exception, and only through the coded
187	  verification form (`verify-in-production`'s probes) — never by asking a session to fetch it.
188	  Where the work is out of reach, do it now, hand it to a routine that has the reach, or do
189	  not file it — and say which.
190	
191	- **Filing an issue that belongs under another** — a phase of a plan, a verification of a change,
192	  a follow-up its parent tracks — attach it as a **sub-issue** (`mcp__github__sub_issue_write`,
193	  method `add`, `sub_issue_id` the **id** the create call returned, not its number), never only a
194	  number named in the body. The parent then carries what is still open under it, in the place a
195	  reader is already looking.
196	
197	- **Handing over a step only a human can perform** (flipping a repository or console setting,
198	  granting a permission, adding a secret) — first confirm you genuinely can't do it yourself, then
199	  give it **its own issue**, never a note in the PR body, with a checkbox per step, what breaks
200	  while each is off, and its closing condition. The exception is a step whose home is an artifact
201	  the human is already editing. How that issue is *written* — the checklist as the whole artifact,
202	  every explanation below it — is
203	  [writing-handover-issues](skills/writing-handover-issues/SKILL.md).
204	
205	# Engineering practices
206	
207	- **Naming a file, module, or symbol** — name it for its scope or responsibility, not the
208	  technology or mechanism behind it.
209	
210	- **Referring to a value from more than one place** — prefer a shared constant or a reference over
211	  copying it, and generate derived data rather than hand-maintaining it. If you can't, add a drift
212	  guard: the generic `sharedConstants` check for a plain value, or one that runs the real logic
213	  against the copy in both directions when the duplicate mirrors matcher or predicate logic. Keep
214	  the guarded literal itself unbroken, since a value split across a line break is invisible to the
215	  guard and to a `grep`/`sed` rename alike. Have the guard's own text name the places it watches and
216	  why the split is forced, and don't also comment the duplication — the guard covers it.
217	
218	- **Writing file A so it depends on file B** — say what A needs from B, or that it delegates, and
219	  don't re-spell how B does its job. If you're about to paraphrase B's procedure, point at B
220	  instead. This holds for code comments and Markdown alike. The test for whether a detail
221	  belongs: if that detail changes, does A actually care? A specific that wouldn't force A to
222	  change — B's cadence, B's file layout, the reasoning behind how B works — is B's detail, not
223	  A's, and doesn't belong in A even as color.
224	
225	- **Writing code that depends on how a platform or runtime behaves** — verify that behaviour
226	  against authoritative docs or a real run, not a comment or a prior commit's claim.
227	
228	- **Optimising** — if the change is meant to preserve behaviour, prove it: hash the full outputs
229	  of both paths across every branch, fuzzing the inputs that select each, and accept only a
230	  bit-identical match. If the correctness risk outweighs the speed-up, leave the path alone and
231	  record that as a deliberate call.
232	
233	- **Needing a library for a narrow job** — prefer a built-in, or a few lines. When the assumption
234	  that justified an existing dependency lapses, drop it.
235	
236	- **Answering an edge case a review raised** — first check whether the existing composed rules
237	  already produce the right answer. If they do, add no production code: pin it with a regression
238	  test that asserts the contrast case too, plus an accept criterion where you track those, and don't
239	  re-state it in a comment.
240	
241	- **Documenting a procedure** — read the authoritative external docs first and write only what
242	  they don't carry: our failure modes, gotchas, the exact path we ran. Don't document or recommend a
243	  path you haven't run, however standard it looks.
244	
245	- **Writing code that can silently do nothing** — a swallowed error, a best-effort fallback, a
246	  probe-gated optimisation, a hint the runtime may ignore — record which path actually ran,
247	  reading the state back where the platform exposes it. During development, before the solution is
248	  proven right, add that debugging information first and remove it later. Without the record, a run
249	  where the capability never engaged is indistinguishable from one where it did and didn't help.
250	
251	- **Persisting anything on a user's machine** — put it under the one user-deletable location, and
252	  extend that location rather than earn a second one. If the platform forces something outside it, a
253	  registration the OS owns, name that explicitly as the exception.
254	
255	- **Changing what the software does with a user's data** — the permission string, privacy policy
256	  and store listing are part of the contract, so change them in the same commit. Retaining something
257	  new, opening a listener or adding an outbound connection changes the promise rather than adding a
258	  field: decide it explicitly and rewrite the disclosure before the code. Expect the claim in more
259	  than one place — grep the whole surface for the standing absolutes it touches ("no tracking",
260	  "no cookies", "no external assets") and reconcile every hit.
261	
262	- **Driving an external runtime more than once in a session** — a headless browser, a device, a
263	  REPL, a deploy target — write one parameterised driver into the scratchpad, taking the target,
264	  the selector and the output path from argv, and re-point it rather than author a throwaway per
265	  invocation.
266	
267	- **Automating something that needs live conversation context** — hook it to an existing human
268	  workflow event rather than background infrastructure; shell hooks have no conversation access and
269	  fire per turn, not at session end. Consider changing an existing command's definition — usually
270	  the cheapest trigger.
271	
272	- **Writing the exit path of a pipeline or CI step** — an expected, handled outcome exits clean
273	  with a comment. Reserve non-zero for genuine breakage.
274	
275	- **Piping a long command's output through `tail` (or `head`) to keep it readable** — it discards
276	  the pipeline's real exit code (`$?` becomes the trailing command's, not the one you're
277	  checking), so a mid-chain failure goes unnoticed, and any earlier summary lines the truncation
278	  cut are gone right when you need them. Redirect to a file (or `tee`) instead, read `$?` from
279	  that same invocation, and grep the file afterward for whatever slice you actually need — never
280	  re-run the whole thing to re-slice its output.
281	
282	- **Killing a process by pattern** — `pkill -f` matches the invoking shell's own command line too,
283	  so never chain it, and bracket one character of the pattern (`[h]ttp.server 8099`) to break the
284	  self-match.
285	
286	- **Working in a fresh checkout or sandbox** — a setup script may start in the repo's parent
287	  rather than the checkout, so `cd` in before running anything. A `Cannot find module` there is
288	  usually an install that hasn't run yet, not a code bug: install and re-run before hunting for a
289	  code-level cause.
290	
291	- **Deciding where a config value or a classification lives** — avoid a default; require the value
292	  explicitly, or make it structural, derived from where the thing lives. Prefer a structural
293	  classifier to a hand-set field, and collapse a property tracked in several places into one. When
294	  automation maintains many copies of a config, have it materialize the explicit value into every
295	  file it maintains instead of interpreting absence.
296	
297	- **Handling a value that can be unknown** — unknown is a state of its own: never encode it as a
298	  zero, an empty string or a type's default, and don't let a decoder collapse it into one. Keep it a
299	  missing key or an explicit null, keep the zero for a real zero, and preserve all three states at
300	  every stage of a pipeline. Treat absence as a permanent shape of the data rather than a gap to
301	  close, and where two fields claim the same fact, let each mean what its own source said and leave
302	  the call to the consumer.
303	
304	- **Writing a comment** — carry the why, or a cross-file relationship the code can't state itself;
305	  if the code plus a known convention already says it, write nothing. Describe the current state,
306	  never the edit that produced it: don't explain the change you just made, and don't note what was
307	  removed or renamed. If a comment narrates a past fix, keep only the part still true of the code in
308	  front of you. When it must name a path, spell that path in one canonical place and point every
309	  other mention there.

1	---
2	name: git-github-advanced
3	description: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
4	---
5	
6	# Portable git & GitHub procedures
7	
8	A GitHub procedure the consuming repo's own docs set — its merge command, when it opens a PR, its generated-file merge rules — wins over anything below.
9	
10	## Updating an issue's status: comment, don't overwrite
11	
12	To post a **status update** on an issue (the lifecycle's "update the issue's status" step), use `add_issue_comment`. **Don't** reach for `issue_write` with `method: update` — that edits the issue itself and **replaces the whole body**, silently wiping the original description. Reserve `issue_write`/`update` for genuinely editing the issue (retitling, rewriting the body on purpose).
13	
14	## An auto-merge refusal is not a verdict — read the PR's state, then act
15	
16	`enable_pr_auto_merge` only accepts a PR whose required checks are still **pending**, so its refusals answer *timing and configuration*, never the change. Take each at face value and stop:
17	
18	- *"already in clean status (all checks passed)"* — the checks finished before you got there. That's the green light: `merge_pull_request` directly.
19	- *"in unstable status (required checks are failing)"* — this same wording covers a check that is **queued** or **held at an approval gate**. Resolve it by reading the PR's check runs and looking at **`status`**, not `conclusion`; a check that hasn't `completed` has no verdict.
20	- *"Protected branch rules not configured"* — auto-merge is a protected-branch feature, so a repo with no rule on its default branch can never arm it. Final; don't let an earlier refusal's wording talk you out of it.
21	
22	Never re-arm on a loop hoping the answer changes — observed runs answered "unstable" then "clean" seconds later with nothing changed in between, and one spent ~6 minutes of a 13-minute budget circling a single PR without merging it.
23	
24	## Don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same commit that deletes what produced its artifacts
25	
26	Removing a toolchain invites tidying away its ignore rules alongside it — but the artifacts it already produced are usually still sitting untracked in the worktree (`__pycache__/` from an earlier run, `build/` from an earlier build). The moment those rules go, the next `git add -A` sweeps the junk *into* the commit that was supposed to remove it, and nothing complains: the commit is valid and the tests still pass. Delete (or `git clean`) the artifacts first, then drop their ignore lines. And after any bulk `git add -A`, read `git diff --cached --stat` — staged additions are exactly what a clean `git status` stops telling you about.
27	
28	## Branch and commit history
29	
30	### Commit often, in layers
31	
32	While working a branch, commit frequently rather than landing one big commit at the end — small, ordered commits let the owner follow the work as it develops. Use commits to *layer* the work in the order you'd want it reviewed:
33	
34	- Write the failing test(s) first, commit them, **then** implement the feature — so the history shows the contract before the code that satisfies it (and you've seen the test fail before trusting it).
35	- Keep any documentation update as its own commit *after* the feature, not folded into it.
36	
37	There's no cost to a branch carrying many commits when the project uses a **squash** merge to `main` (one commit per PR): the squash collapses them into a single commit on `main`, so `main`'s one-commit-per-PR history is unaffected no matter how granularly the branch is committed.
38	
39	- **One caveat, at merge time: before rebasing an *unmerged* multi-commit branch onto a *moved* base, collapse commits that rewrite the same lines into one.** When your own commits churn the same lines (build X → refactor → remove X, common in an iterative design session) and the base has advanced, rebasing the stack replays *every* intermediate conflict against the new base. The squash-merge discards those commits anyway, so collapse them first — `git reset --soft $(git merge-base HEAD origin/main)` then one fresh commit, and rebase that single commit: one conflict pass, not N. Lossless (unlike `reset --hard` + redo) and simpler than `--onto` when you want a single commit anyway.
40	
41	- **When a rebase or a review round drops part of a branch, amend the commit message in the same step** — then read it back against `git show --stat` before merging. Under a squash merge the branch's commit body *becomes* `main`'s permanent record, while the explanation of what was dropped, if it lives in a PR comment, is not carried by the squash at all. A commit describing a change to files it never touched sends the next reader of `git log -- <path>` hunting for work that isn't there.
42	
43	- Don't rewrite published/shared history to satisfy a tooling or authorship check (e.g. a hook flagging "unverified" commits): only amend your own un-pushed branch commits. Commits already on a shared branch — including ones merged in from `main` — belong to that history; reset-authoring or rebasing them forks your branch away from it.
44	- After your commit is **squash-merged** to `main`, a *reused* feature branch still carries that original commit (the squash created a *new* commit on `main`, so the branch's own is unreachable from it) — and the next PR off the branch re-includes it in the diff, because the three-dot merge-base predates the squash. Sync the branch to `origin/main` before opening the next PR (`git rebase origin/main`, which drops the commit as an already-applied cherry-pick, or a hard reset): it's your own un-merged branch, so this is the amend-your-own-commits case above, not rewriting shared history.
45	  - **`git rebase origin/main` only drops the old commit cleanly when the branch carried a *single* squash-merged commit.** When it carried *several* commits that `main` squashed into *one* (then kept developing), git can't match them to the squash as already-applied, so it replays them and conflicts mid-rebase. Replant only the genuinely-new commits instead: `git rebase --onto origin/main <last-squash-merged-commit>` (then `git push --force-with-lease`). If the new work is small, a `git reset --hard origin/main` + redo beats fighting the replay.
46	  - **If the merge auto-deleted the remote branch, start follow-up work on a new branch off `origin/main`** rather than reusing the old name — it has no stale tracking ref and no rebase dance. If you do reuse the old name: `--force-with-lease` actively *fails* — `git push --force-with-lease` rejects with `stale info` then `couldn't find remote ref <branch>` because the lease expects a remote branch that no longer exists. There's nothing to overwrite, so `git fetch --prune` (drop the stale tracking ref) then a plain `git push -u origin <branch>` just recreates it.
47	
48	## An automated commit-nag is not authorization to commit drift
49	
50	An automated prompt to commit the working tree (a stop-hook, a CI nag) tells you the tree is dirty — not that the changes are yours or intended. Before obeying, inspect what actually changed (`git status` / `git diff`): if it's environment/setup drift — a submodule pointer moved by `git submodule update` at clone time, a lockfile a setup script regenerated, generated artifacts — revert it rather than committing it onto your branch. Committing drift slips an unintended dependency or generated-file bump into an unrelated change.
51	
52	## Open a PR early when the reviewable artifact only exists on CI
53	
54	The default is to hold a PR until asked. Reverse that when a change's only reviewable output is produced by CI — an e2e/heavy-browser run, or a rendered artifact (a UI-snapshot pixel diff, a generated gallery) that can't be exercised in the local sandbox. Opening the PR is how the change is seen working and how failures surface, so doing it up front — rather than iterating locally first, which proves nothing for these classes — is the faster path to a working, reviewable result. Each CI iteration costs a full round-trip, so get the first one running as early as possible.
55	
56	## Never `git checkout <ref> -- <paths>` to carry uncommitted edits onto another branch
57	
58	It reads those paths out of `<ref>`'s **committed** tree and writes them over the working copy — so the uncommitted edits you were trying to move are destroyed, silently and unrecoverably (no reflog, no stash). Move in-progress work either by branching in place (`git checkout -b <new>`, which carries a dirty tree with it) or by committing/stashing first and then restoring on the new branch. In particular never put the checkout in the same `&&` chain as the branch creation: by the time it runs, the edits are already the only copy.
59	
60	## Sync early to keep merge conflicts small
61	
62	Conflict size scales with how long a branch lives and how far it drifts from the default branch. Sync early rather than at the end: when starting work on a branch — and periodically while it's open — bring the latest default branch in first, so the branch carries current sources instead of discovering the gap at merge time. A one-commit-per-PR squash history already keeps each branch a single reviewable unit, so shorter-lived, freshly-synced branches are the norm.
63	
64	**In a repo that forbids merge commits on the branch — the `squash-merge-history` check, or squash-only merging generally — sync by *rebasing*, never `git merge` the base in.** A `git merge origin/main` (even just to resolve conflicts) leaves a **merge commit** the check blocks, forcing a redo; `git pull --rebase` / `git rebase origin/main` replays your work with no merge commit. GitHub's **"Update branch"** button — and the `update_pull_request_branch` API behind it — is this same base-merge in disguise: it adds exactly the merge commit the check blocks, so refresh with a local rebase + `git push --force-with-lease` instead. The merge-conflict-resolution gotchas below apply to a rebase's conflicts exactly the same way.
65	
66	## A local git-mutation refusal after a merge already succeeded server-side is not worth a second variant
67	
68	Once an API call reports the merge done (`merged: true`), syncing your local checkout afterward is a convenience, not part of landing it — so if the session's own permission/auto-mode classifier denies a mutating git command (`git checkout main`, `git pull`, `git reset --hard`), take one attempt and stop; a differently-phrased retry (a plain `checkout`, then `fetch origin main`, then `reset --hard`) hits the same classifier and burns minutes on a step with nothing downstream of it. State plainly that local `main` is behind and move on, or confirm what's needed **read-only** (`git log`, a file-contents fetch against the server) instead of continuing to mutate.
69	
70	## The sandbox checkout can be shallow, and a shallow history breaks `git merge-base`
71	
72	A shallow clone (or a shallow default checkout in a sandboxed session) carries a truncated history graph with synthetic grafts, so `git merge-base <default> <branch>` fails for branches that predate the shallow point — even ordinary, cleanly-merged ones — and any check that reads that failure as "orphaned" or "unrelated" produces false positives at scale. Before trusting a merge-base result (or any cross-branch history comparison), run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`; if it reads `true`, unshallow first: `git fetch origin '+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*' --prune && git fetch --unshallow`.
73	
74	## Prefer `git commit && git push` over the MCP file-write tools for a file already correct on disk
75	
76	`push_files`/`create_or_update_file` take the file body as a literal string the model composes for the call, so what lands is a **transcription** of the file, not the file — a truncated JSON config and a stray inserted blank line have both landed this way on real PRs, each caught only by chance. Reserve the MCP write path for what genuinely needs it (a file a scoped token can push but the session's own git remote can't — e.g. `.github/workflows/` under a `GITHUB_TOKEN` that's forbidden to push it), and when you do use it, read the result back with a file-contents fetch and diff it against the local copy before moving on.
77	
78	## A run that never executed the repo's own steps is infrastructure, not a CI failure to wait out
79	
80	Two tells: a check stuck `queued` that auto-cancels around 15 minutes with its job logs then 404ing, or a job that dies in an early platform-provided step (e.g. "Prepare all required actions" / "Failed to resolve action download info … Service Unavailable") before your own workflow's steps ever start. Recognize the pattern and say plainly that it's a platform outage rather than continuing to poll or hunting for a repo-side cause — re-running (once) is the whole remedy; waiting longer or diagnosing the workflow file spends more time on an outage neither can fix.
81	
82	## After a remote-side merge, fetch before branching off origin/main
83	
84	A GitHub API/UI (or any remote-side) merge does **not** advance your local `origin/main` — it stays at the pre-merge commit until you `git fetch`. Branching off `origin/main` immediately after a remote merge forks the pre-merge state, silently missing the just-merged work; symptoms surface later as a missing file or a failed `git mv` on the new branch. Fix: `git fetch origin main` before creating the branch.
85	
86	## `git pull` failing "refusing to merge unrelated histories" usually means upstream re-rooted
87	
88	When syncing a long-lived local clone's default branch fails with `refusing to merge unrelated histories` (often alongside `ahead N, behind M`), the usual cause is that upstream **re-rooted** the branch — a history rewrite replaced the root commit — not repository corruption. Do **not** reach for `--allow-unrelated-histories`: that "fix" welds the two histories together into a merge nobody wants. Instead inspect what the local side uniquely holds (`git log origin/<branch>..<branch>` — typically just the old root), keep anything real by rebasing it onto the new history, then `git reset --hard origin/<branch>`. A work branch created from *fetched* refs is unaffected; only stale local refs from before the rewrite hit this.
89	
90	## A conformance finding on history you didn't write may be a stale diff base — refresh before fixing
91	
92	A Stop-hook or CI conformance check diffs your branch against `origin/main`. In a fresh cloud sandbox that ref can be **stale** — behind real `main` by whole merged PRs — so the check reads the wrong base and can flag findings on commits or code you never touched. Before acting on a finding you don't recognize, `git fetch origin <default-branch>` and re-run: a stale-base phantom disappears, and whatever survives against the current base is real — fix that. (The same stale ref bases new work on outdated product code, so fetch before building against `main`, too.)
93	
94	The same reflex applies when a **real** (not phantom) red check blocks *your* PR and you've correctly pinned it as pre-existing and unrelated to your diff: that "not mine" diagnosis is a **sync-the-base** signal, not a fix-it-yourself-or-ask-the-user one — `main` has often *already fixed* it since you branched, so merge/rebase the latest base into your branch and re-check before proposing a fix or escalating.
95	
96	## In a squash-merge repo, "commits ahead of main" does not mean "unmerged"
97	
98	A squash-merge creates a new commit on `main` that the branch's own commits are unreachable from, so a branch whose work has already landed still shows ahead by N. **"Ahead by N" never alone means unmerged.** Determine real status by content, not raw count:
99	
100	1. **PR state** — a merged PR means the work is in `main`; safe to delete however many commits show ahead.
101	2. **Content diff** — `git diff --stat main..branch`: if everything the branch adds is already in `main`, the work landed (catches a squash with no surviving PR).
102	3. **Superseded elsewhere** — the branch's work may have landed in `main` under a *different path or form* (a doc distilled into another, a feature re-implemented), so a file/line diff still shows its additions as branch-side and it reads as unmerged. Before concluding so, check whether its *intent* already exists in `main` — grep for the concept, not just the exact path.
103	4. **No merge-base** — `git merge-base` fails when a force-push rewrote `main` and orphaned the branch; can't be proven in or out mechanically; needs human review, never an automatic delete.
104	5. Otherwise — genuine unmerged work.
105	
106	## A push or PR made with the Actions `GITHUB_TOKEN` does not start another workflow
107	
108	GitHub suppresses workflow runs triggered by the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to prevent recursion, so a workflow's own `git push` or `gh pr create` won't fire another workflow (e.g. a `test` or cache-refresh workflow). The one exception is `workflow_dispatch` / `repository_dispatch` — which is why an automation pipeline that needs the downstream checks to run must dispatch them explicitly. A run dispatched against a branch executes on its head commit, so its checks still attach to the PR. The same suppression covers a Claude session's own app-scoped pushes: creating a PR through the API does fire its `pull_request` run, but a follow-up push to that PR gets **no** `synchronize` run — so don't wait for checks that will never start on the new head; gate by running the CI commands locally, and rely on the post-merge run (merging through the merge API does fire the `push` workflow on the default branch).
109	
110	**"Suppressed" is not always "absent", and the difference decides whether a PR can merge.** Where the repo requires approval for a workflow run, GitHub *creates* the `pull_request` run and parks it at conclusion `action_required` with **zero jobs**, waiting for a human "Approve and run" that unattended automation never gets. The run never executes and never reports, yet it still counts against the PR: `mergeable_state` stays `unstable` and auto-merge refuses to arm, even though the explicitly dispatched run on the same head sha passed. Nothing inside the workflow file can prevent it — `branches`/`branches-ignore` on `pull_request` filter the **base** branch (a bot branch's PR still targets the default branch), and the approval gate is applied to the whole run before any job-level `if` is evaluated. So treat a gated run as **no verdict rather than a failure**, and land the PR on the evidence of the run that actually ran.
111	
112	## A workflow definition only takes effect once it's on the default branch
113	
114	A `workflow_dispatch` or scheduled workflow runs from the copy on the **default branch**, and a `pull_request` run uses the workflow files from the PR's **base** branch — so a workflow you only added on a feature branch isn't dispatchable, and a build/CI change doesn't apply, until it's merged. Merge workflow and build-script changes *before* the release or run that depends on them, or that run executes the *old* definition (shipping a stale build, or silently skipping a check you thought you'd added). This is distinct from the `GITHUB_TOKEN` recursion rule above: even a human-triggered run reads the definition from the default/base branch, not your feature branch.
115	
116	## A CI OIDC `sub` claim is matched case-sensitively by the cloud trust policy
117	
118	GitHub's OIDC `sub` uses the repository's **canonical casing** (`repo:Owner/Repo:ref:…`), and a cloud trust policy compares it exactly — AWS IAM `StringEquals` is case-sensitive — so a trust policy written with the wrong case fails with a bare `Not authorized to perform sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` and **no** hint that casing is the cause. Match the exact canonical `owner/repo` (or list both casings in the condition). The same exact-match caution applies to any OIDC-federated cloud, not just AWS.
119	
120	## An automated job needs a unique branch per run
121	
122	An automated or scheduled job that derives its branch name from a non-unique key (e.g. the date) collides with itself on a repeat run for that key — `git checkout -b` fails when the branch already exists, and a push to the diverged remote branch is rejected non-fast-forward (so the run can't even open its PR). Give every run its own branch: append a per-run-unique suffix (`$RANDOM` / a short token) to the readable prefix.
123	
124	## An unattended workflow must escalate its own failure to a human-visible state
125	
126	A workflow with no human watching the run — scheduled, triggered by a push/merge, or a fire-and-forget manual dispatch, with no other path that reaches a person — must converge a failure to something a human will see (e.g. open a `workflow-failure` issue for it) rather than merely exiting red in the Actions list, where nobody looks. Skip this only when the failure is already loud: a `pull_request`/push CI run that blocks merge with a red required check the author is watching, or a workflow that already flags the triggering issue itself on failure. The canon's [report-failure](../../../../.github/actions/report-failure/action.yml) action does exactly this — a **fresh** issue per failure, with earlier open failure issues for the same workflow closed as duplicates of the newest — so the current failure is always the single open bug to triage; a standing per-workflow issue appended to on each failure is an equally valid shape, the invariant is only that the red run reaches a person.
127	
128	When the escalation is itself a separate reusable workflow invoked via `workflow_call`, permissions don't propagate implicitly through the chain: the job that calls it needs the permission explicitly granted (e.g. `issues: write`), and if that reusable workflow in turn calls another one, the middle workflow must forward the same grant to its own call — a caller two levels up granting it once is not enough.
129	
130	## A CI job that inspects commit shape must check out the PR head, not the merge ref
131	
132	On `pull_request`, `actions/checkout` checks out the synthetic `refs/pull/N/merge` commit by default — an ephemeral merge of the PR head into the base — so `HEAD` is itself a merge commit, not the branch tip. Any job that reasons about commit *shape* or history (merge commits, commit count, `--first-parent`, commit messages) reads that synthetic merge and misfires: a "no merge commits" check false-positives even on a linear branch, since `HEAD` is a merge. Check out the head SHA (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}`) so CI evaluates the same branch tip a local run does.
133	
134	## To read a PR's CI result, look at its check runs — `get_status` misses Actions
135	
136	GitHub **Actions** reports results as **check runs**, not the legacy **commit statuses**, so `pull_request_read` `method: get_status` returns `state: pending`, `total_count: 0` for a PR whose Actions CI has already **passed** — reading falsely as "no CI / not started," which can skip a real gate or trigger an endless wait. Gate on CI by reading the **check runs for the PR head SHA** (`get_check_run`, or the workflow run for that SHA) instead. Target the head SHA directly rather than `actions_list`-ing the repo's runs — that returns every run, its output is huge, and a specific check-run/SHA query is both correct and cheap.
137	
138	## To confirm a non-PR run (push / dispatch), read its job logs — it has no PR check runs
139	
140	A `push` or `workflow_dispatch` run isn't attached to a PR, so the PR-scoped check-run query above doesn't apply to it. Confirm such a run through the GitHub API/MCP tools: `get_job_logs(run_id, failed_only: true)` — "0 failed jobs" means green — or, for a release build, `get_release_by_tag`. `get_job_logs` needs more than a bare `run_id`: it rejects with "job_id is required when failed_only is false" unless you pass `failed_only: true` or fetch a `job_id` first (`list_workflow_jobs`), and it 404s for a job still `in_progress` — wait for the job to finish. Don't `curl` the run's status instead: in a sandboxed session `api.github.com` is proxy-blocked and returns an error body that never matches a success pattern, so a `curl`/`Monitor` poll silently reports "still running" until it times out.
141	
142	## A deleted workflow's old runs outlive it, and no session tool can clear them
143	
144	Removing a `.yml` from every branch does not remove its run history — the workflow stays listed in
145	the Actions tab, a ghost registration attached only to runs that already happened. Clearing it
146	needs `DELETE /repos/.../actions/runs/{run_id}`, an `actions: write` endpoint outside the read/
147	list/get-logs/dispatch surface the GitHub MCP toolset exposes. Don't hunt for a session-side fix
148	that doesn't exist — hand the cleanup to the owner (their own UI, or a one-time sanctioned
149	workflow) instead.
150	
151	## A green run is not evidence its job ran — read the job's own conclusion
152	
153	A workflow that gates a later job (an `if:` on changed paths, a mode flag, a preceding job's output) concludes **success** with that job **skipped** — so "the release workflow is green" is not evidence the publish step ever executed, and most green runs may never have reached it. Read the conclusion of the **job that does the thing**, never the run's. The corollary for closing an issue: the only closing evidence is a run that actually reached that job and went green, or the external system showing the effect. Fixing a repo-side defect that merely co-occurred with the failure verifies nothing, and a failure caused by state in an external service has no fix in the repo at all.
154	
155	## Mark large committed fixtures `linguist-vendored` to fix language stats
156	
157	Large committed fixture files (full-page HTML, generated data dumps) can dwarf actual source by byte count and cause GitHub to mislabel the repo's primary language. Add a `.gitattributes` entry for each such path (e.g. `test/fixtures/*.html linguist-vendored`) to tell Linguist to ignore it; apply the same annotation whenever you add another large generated or fixture file.
158	
159	## Renaming a directory that houses a submodule
160	
161	`git mv` on a directory containing a submodule rewrites `.gitmodules` and the index correctly but leaves `.git/config` stale — its old `[submodule "<old/path>"]` entry lingers, so any operation that consults `.git/config` (submodule status, checkout) sees the old path until you fix it. Run `git submodule sync && git submodule update --init` after the move to propagate the new path and re-register the submodule.
162	
163	## GitHub Markdown inside a `<td>` requires surrounding blank lines
164	
165	In a GitHub-rendered Markdown file, cmark-gfm re-enters Markdown mode inside a raw `<td>` only when blank lines surround the cell's content — without them the cell is treated as a raw HTML block and its content is shown verbatim (no `![img]()`, no `**bold**`, no links). GitHub's sanitizer strips `style` / CSS, so a flexbox two-column layout won't render; use a plain `<table>` with `align` / `valign` / `width` instead. GFM pipe-table cells can't hold multi-line prose — use the raw-`<table>` form when a cell needs it. A leading inline `<!-- … -->` comment also opens an HTML block, so keep any such marker as the *last* token on the line, leaving the line to *start* as Markdown.
166	
167	## `commit.gpgsign = true` does not cover merge commits
168	
169	`commit.gpgsign = true` signs ordinary commits but does not apply to `git merge` — each merge produces an unsigned commit even with signing fully configured. In a repo that enforces commit verification, this requires a fix-up after the fact. Cover merges proactively: either pass `-S` to every `git merge` call, or set `merge.gpgsign = true` globally so merges are signed the same way commits are.
170	
171	## When access is scoped to an explicit repo list, query per-repo — never an org/user-wide search
172	
173	A broad call (e.g. `search_repositories` with `org:X`, or any list/search tool that takes no repo argument) returns every repo the token can see, not just an allowed subset — filtering the result afterward doesn't undo the fact that disallowed repos' data was already pulled into the call. When operating under a repo allowlist, scope every call explicitly instead: pass the specific `owner`/`repo` params, or anchor the query to `repo:owner/name`, one call per repo in the allowlist rather than one broad call filtered after the fact.
174	
175	## Cap *and* qualify every list/search call — an unbounded one blows the tool-result limit
176	
177	A list or search API call that isn't bounded returns a full page of full-bodied records and overruns the agent's tool-result cap, which costs two or three further calls to dig the answer back out of the spilled result — a pure-overhead round trip on a call whose wanted answer was a single record. Two independent bounds, both needed:
178	
179	- **Qualify the query so it matches what you mean.** A bare string handed to an issue/PR search is a *full-text* search over the whole repo — title, body, and comments — so a lookup for one known issue returns every issue that merely mentions the phrase, each with its whole body. Anchor it to the field (`in:title "<exact title>"`), or use the narrower tool (a label-filtered `list_issues`, a run-id or head-SHA query) instead of a search.
180	- **When you already know the exact title, don't search at all — list and match it yourself.** Field anchoring is a *GitHub search API* feature, and an MCP layer in front of it may match **semantically** instead, ranking by resemblance and honouring no qualifier: the title you named can then rank below unrelated issues or be absent from the page entirely, and `in:title` changes nothing. Enumerate with `list_issues` (a narrow field list, a large page size, no state filter — a log issue is often deliberately closed) and compare the string in-session. Reserve search for what it is good at: finding items you can only *describe*.
181	- **Trim the fields, not just the page size.** The per-object field set is what governs the payload, so capping the page can leave the response byte-identical — measured, the same call at two page sizes returned output identical to the character. Ask for the fields you need (`["number","title","state"]` covers most lookups); dropping the body alone is usually the whole difference. Where a tool offers no field selection, narrow the query instead, or take the overflow as the answer and read the spilled result file directly rather than retrying it smaller.
182	- **Pass a small explicit page size.** Default page sizes are tuned for a browser, not a tool result; when the answer wanted is one issue or one run, ask for 5–10, never a bare unpaged call.
183	
184	All of them, not one: a qualified query still returns a full page, a small page of unqualified matches is still the wrong records, and a small page of full-bodied records still overruns the cap.
185	
186	## Merging gotchas
187	
188	These conflict/merge traps are independent of any one project's file layout.
189	
190	### Merging across a file relocation
191	
192	git's rename detection re-applies your content edits onto the moved files, but it does *not* fix *references* to the moved paths — an npm script, a `.gitattributes` glob, or a doc link naming the old location keeps pointing there and breaks with no conflict (a green local test on the old layout won't catch it either). After such a merge, grep the files your branch touched for the old paths.
193	
194	### Merging in content that predates a branch-wide invariant
195	
196	When your branch establishes a cross-cutting invariant — a renamed term, a "mentioned only in X" containment rule — a branch you merge in that *predates* it can silently reintroduce violations: its independent additions (a new file, a new section) auto-merge clean, no conflict, while still using the old form. Resolving the marked conflicts isn't enough. Re-run the check that *defines* the invariant (the grep) over the whole tree after the merge, not just the conflicted files.
197	
198	### Porting old work forward across a changed invariant
199	
200	The converse direction: when you re-implement or cherry-pick an *older* change onto current `main`, check each part against the invariants `main` has added since — not just whether it still applies. A part that violates a now-enforced guarantee becomes a **silent no-op** if taken verbatim (e.g. a guard that reverts any write outside an allowed set leaves the patch landed but doing nothing), so drop or redesign it rather than copy it.
201

1	---
2	name: github-actions-scheduling
3	description: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
4	---
5	
6	# GitHub Actions cron is best-effort
7	
8	GitHub's `schedule:` trigger is a **request to queue**, not a promise to run. A cron'd workflow
9	routinely fires minutes to tens of minutes late, and under load GitHub **drops** a firing
10	outright — the run never happens, with no failure, no notification, and nothing in the run
11	ledger to look at. The effect is worst at `:00` and other round minutes, where everyone's cron
12	lands at once. GitHub's docs concede only that a schedule "may be delayed during periods of high
13	loads"; the behaviour is measured across a fleet in
14	[Upptime's write-up](https://upptime.js.org/blog/2021/01/22/github-actions-schedule-not-working/).
15	Same family, different mechanism: GitHub **disables** a repo's scheduled workflows entirely
16	after 60 days without repository activity.
17	
18	## Building for it
19	
20	- **Never let correctness depend on a firing happening, or on when it happened.** Derive what is
21	  due from durable state the run can read — the Actions run ledger, a timestamp in the repo, the
22	  world the job inspects — never from "this fired, so it must be time". Wall-clock equality with
23	  the cron minute is not a test any real run passes.
24	- **Idempotent and self-catching.** A scheduled job does whatever is outstanding *now*, so a
25	  missed firing costs latency rather than data. Per-scheduler run bookkeeping — counters, "the last hour's
26	  changes", a queue advanced one step per run — loses information the first time a scheduler run vanishes.
27	  If a job cannot catch up, say so where it is declared and design the miss as an accepted loss.
28	- **Catch up the most recent slot only.** A job that backfills every missed slot turns an outage
29	  into a storm on recovery; one catch-up evaluation per frequency is the shape that survives a
30	  multi-day gap.
31	- **Spacing two jobs apart is not an ordering.** "B is an hour after A, so A has finished by
32	  then" holds only while the fires land on time — and when a poll is dropped, the catch-up run
33	  finds *both* due and does them together, which is precisely the run where B most needs A to
34	  have gone first. If the order actually matters, assert it in the run: have the run do A and
35	  defer B, or have B check for A's result and skip when it is missing. Spacing is a preference;
36	  a check is a guarantee.
37	- **Pick a minute off `:00`.** Anywhere in `:10–:50` dodges the stampede and stays clear of the
38	  hour boundary any slot math anchors on; across a fleet, hash the repo name into that band so
39	  members spread rather than collide.
40	- **Deadline-bound work does not belong on a cron.** If something must happen *at* a time, drive
41	  it from the event, not an hourly poll that may skip.
42	
43	## Talking about it
44	
45	- **Say "about hourly, best-effort", never "hourly".** Stating an interval the platform does not
46	  honour turns ordinary jitter into a bug report.
47	- **A late or missing run is not a defect until proven one.** First question: did GitHub fire at
48	  all — check the workflow's run list, not the job's logic. Then: has the repo been quiet for 60
49	  days? Only after both does the code become a suspect. A single missed slot is expected
50	  behaviour.
51	
52	Claudinite's own scheduler is built to this: a repo-hashed `:10–:50` minute, and an hourly scheduler run
53	that reconciles a queue of issues rather than replaying a ledger — a missed fire leaves the queue
54	exactly as it was, so the next one catches up by looking at it. See
55	[the writing-tasks skill](../../../claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md) for the task-authoring side.
56

1	---
2	name: merge-to-main
3	description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-tool-calls:
6	    - 'mcp__github__merge_pull_request'
7	  force-load-on-prompts-matching:
8	    - '/\bLGTM\b/'
9	---
10	
11	# Merge to main
12	
13	If the project's own `CLAUDE.md` names a merge-policy file, that file overrides the divergent
14	points below (merge method, CI gating). Don't go hunting for one it doesn't name.
15	
16	1. Load `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request` in one `ToolSearch`.
17	2. No PR open for the branch? `create_pull_request` (base `main`), body ending `Closes #<issue>`.
18	3. If the PR has check runs, wait for them to pass. None — merge without waiting.
19	4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Don't pre-read
20	   mergeability; the call fails loudly.
21	5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.
22	6. Capture the conversation:
23	   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
24	   (in the canon repo: `node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`). Skip only if
25	   the repo doesn't declare `claudinite-growth`. A later merge in the same session runs it
26	   again. (1)
27	7. Run the basics pack's
28	   [verify-in-production](../../../basics/skills/verify-in-production/SKILL.md) skill, unasked.
29	   This step is that skill's **only** trigger — it files against what the squash actually landed,
30	   which is why it runs here and not when the code was written or the PR opened. It decides
31	   whether this change needs a production check at all — most don't — and files the issue that
32	   comes back once the change is live. Never offer the owner to check later instead.
33	
34	Don't re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge.
35

1	# core — working with Claudinite itself
2	
3	- **Reading a rule, check or skill that arrived from Claudinite** — it is vendored, under
4	  `.claudinite/shared/`, and the update flows replace that whole tree. Never edit anything there:
5	  change it in the canon, or carry the difference in this repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`.
6	
7	- **Finding a mounted skill, or following a link from inside one you already loaded** — a canon
8	  skill lives at `.claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`; there is no flat
9	  `.claudinite/shared/skills/`. When the `Skill` tool announces a per-session flat "base directory"
10	  (e.g. `.claude/skills/<name>/`) that holds only that one `SKILL.md`, any relative link the
11	  skill's own text carries (to a sibling doc, a sibling skill) was written for its real home and
12	  dangles from that announced base — resolve such links against the canon path instead.
13	
14	- **Wanting a pack's rules to apply here** — declare its id in `.claudinite-settings.json`. Nothing
15	  activates by being mounted, fingerprinted or present on disk, so a pack whose files you can see
16	  but whose id is undeclared contributes no prose, no checks, no skills and no tasks.
17	
18	- **Adding a pack** — run the `adopt-pack` skill, which declares it, asks its adoption questions,
19	  re-vendors and scaffolds. Never hand-copy a pack's content into the repo.
20	
21	- **Setting a project up on Claudinite for the first time** — the `adopt-claudinite` skill.
22	
23	- **Deciding which pack owns a lesson** — read `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`, the catalog of
24	  *every* canon pack, never the mounted subset: the mount holds only what this repo declares, so the
25	  pack that owns the territory may be absent and invisible. When the owning pack is merely too
26	  narrow, widen its `ruleRoutingGuidance.belongs` rather than opening a local pack beside it.
27	
28	- **Judging whether Claudinite is current here** — read the stamp's `engineVersion` and
29	  `packVersions`, never `claudinite.updated` or `ref`: the versioned flows stamp versions and
30	  nothing else, so those two hold the provenance of the last full re-vendor rather than of this
31	  mount, and a member converging nightly reads as weeks stale.
32	
33	- **Answering "why did the mount not update"** — read the member's own artifacts (its declaration,
34	  its stamp, the head sha's runs) before theorizing about a platform setting; propose a settings
35	  change as a conclusion, never as a diagnosis.
36

1	---
2	name: adopt-claudinite
3	description: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
4	---
5	
6	Follow [bootstrap.md](../../../../bootstrap.md)'s **fast path** — canonical there, and idempotent
7	by design. Everything mechanical is one `bootstrap.mjs` invocation from the fetched canon, so the
8	adoption is seven steps: open the adoption issue **first** (the work-scope sweep blocks a commit
9	that references no issue), fetch the canon and run the script, ask **every** pending interview
10	question it reports in one batched `AskUserQuestion` pass (up to 4 per call, the project-class
11	question folded in) and record the answers via `--answer` re-runs, **create the executor routine
12	and write its endpoint into the declaration** (Part 6 — this session's work, and before the
13	commit so it lands in the same PR), land the adoption as one commit referencing the issue,
14	capture the adoption session itself once the PR lands (the fast path's capture step — no
15	SessionEnd hook was loaded when this session started, so nothing else will), then file **one
16	issue** carrying the script's HANDOVER block, a checkbox per step. Never re-enact the doc's parts
17	step by step — they document what the script converges.
18	
19	Two things the fast path spells out and a session keeps getting wrong. A fresh project's
20	interview takes **two** passes, because declaring the project-class pack pulls in a `requires`
21	closure whose questions cannot exist until it is declared — and never more, because an answer is
22	stored verbatim, so an open-ended one needs no clarifying popup. And the executor routine is
23	**unfinished, not human-only**: `create_trigger` makes it, the SETUP block in its own prompt
24	carries the model and repo binding the API cannot set, and only the `CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN` secret is
25	a step the hand-over issue takes. (1)
26	
27	Bootstrap is the one place `apply-vendor-set.mjs` is the right tool, and only because the repo is at
28	version zero: it stamps every declared pack at the newest version, and with no older state there is
29	nothing to skip. Read the next section before reaching for it anywhere else.
30	
31	**Refreshing** an already-vendored repo is **not** a session's job, and must not be hand-rolled.
32	Force the repo's own update task and let the flow do it — through the **GitHub MCP tools**, which is
33	the surface a session actually has (an unattended or web session carries no `gh` CLI, and `curl` to
34	`api.github.com` is proxy-blocked there, so a shell recipe fails exactly where this is most needed):
35	
36	```
37	actions_run_trigger(method: "run_workflow", owner: …, repo: …,
38	                    workflow_id: "claudinite-scheduler.yml",
39	                    ref: "main",                                  # see below
40	                    inputs: { wake: "update" })
41	```
42	
43	`ref` is the **default branch**, not whatever branch you are on: a `workflow_dispatch` always runs the
44	workflow definition from the default branch, so dispatching against a feature branch neither picks up
45	a workflow you only added there nor changes which definition runs. In a local session with `gh`
46	authenticated, `gh workflow run claudinite-scheduler.yml -f wake=update` is the same call.
47	
48	Then **watch it to a terminal state** — a forced run is how you see a change to scheduled machinery
49	work *now*, and parking it on "check tomorrow" is the failure this lever exists to prevent. A
50	dispatched run is not attached to a PR, so read it with `get_job_logs(run_id, failed_only: true)`
51	("0 failed jobs" means green) rather than any PR-scoped check query.
52	
53	**Never refresh a stamped repo by running `apply-vendor-set.mjs` against it.** It advances every
54	declared pack's stamp to the newest version without applying the records in between, and
55	`migrationApplies` is `want > have` — so each record it skips stops applying *permanently*, not just
56	this cycle. The repo is left claiming a version whose shape it was never migrated into, and because
57	the stamp is the only thing that remembers, nothing downstream can tell. This is silent, and it does
58	not self-heal.
59	
60	The update flow exists precisely because a refresh is more than laying files down: it applies the
61	version-ranged records, opens one reviewable PR, withholds anything bound for `.github/workflows/`
62	that the Action token cannot write, and ends at the apply stage when a record's rules need a reader.
63	A session that re-vendors by hand does none of that while looking like it succeeded.
64	
65	**Never** hand-convert a legacy (fetch-at-session-start) member to the
66	vendored mount — that conversion is the gated flip note the nightly applies
67	([vendoring/DESIGN.md](../../../../vendoring/DESIGN.md), phase 2); until then legacy members are maintained
68	per bootstrap.md's transition appendix.
69

1	---
2	name: adopt-pack
3	description: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
4	---
5	
6	Turn one or more packs on: declare, answer what the pack asks, materialize its content, satisfy what
7	it now demands. The declaration is authoritative — declaring is the project's call. Whole-repo
8	bootstrap and the on-demand refresh are [adopt-claudinite](../adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md)'s.
9	
10	## 1. Declare
11	
12	The full directory of adoptable packs — every canon pack with what it covers, how it activates,
13	and what it requires — is vendored in the mount at `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md`
14	(canon-side: `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`); read it when choosing, or when the owner asks what
15	could be added. **Match the owner's plain-words name to a pack id yourself** before asking them to
16	disambiguate — pack ids rarely read like how people describe them, so read the candidate's entry
17	there and confirm the fit.
18	
19	Add each chosen pack's id to `packs` in `.claudinite-settings.json`. A pack that only makes sense
20	alongside another names it in `requires`; `resolveDeclaredPacks` pulls that closure in when the
21	declaration is written, so you declare what you *chose* and its dependencies follow (e.g.
22	`spec-driven-product` pulls `executable-requirements`). An unknown pack name — or an unknown
23	property on an entry — is a blocking **settings** error, not a conformance finding; fix the name.
24	
25	## 2. Interview — the part that is easy to skip and must not be
26	
27	A pack that needs the project's intent before it can provide value declares `questions` on its
28	manifest (see [packs/README.md](../../../README.md) and the machinery in
29	[../adopt-claudinite/interview.mjs](../adopt-claudinite/interview.mjs)). For **every** newly
30	declared pack that asks questions:
31	
32	- Where a question says the repo may already hold the answer (a product brief, an existing
33	  requirements doc, the issue tracker), **read that first and confirm** rather than asking cold.
34	- Otherwise ask the owner directly (`AskUserQuestion`), one question at a time, at the point of
35	  adoption — when a human asked for the adoption, they are present by construction.
36	- Record each answer **verbatim** on that pack's entry as `answers: { "<question-id>": "<text>" }`.
37	  `"n/a — none wanted"` is a valid answer and stops the asking. Where the question carries a
38	  `distill` note, derive the entry's `config` from the answer (e.g. `executable-requirements`'s
39	  spec path → `config.spec`).
40	
41	### When nobody is there to ask
42	
43	Adoption also runs **unattended** — a scheduled task acting on a recommendation, the
44	fleet-add-missing-packs task's agent stage, any run with no human in the loop. The interview is then the hard stop, and
45	the order matters:
46	
47	1. **Never guess an answer, and never leave the question unrecorded.** A pack whose question is
48	   answered by inference carries a decision nobody made, in a file that then propagates by
49	   `requires` closure and outlives whoever could have corrected it. `"n/a"` is an *owner's* answer,
50	   not a default you may write on their behalf.
51	2. **Finish everything the question does not gate, first** — declare, re-vendor, scaffold, and get
52	   the checks green (§4, §5). Stopping at the question with a red repo hands the owner a broken
53	   tree *and* a question; stopping with a green one hands them only the question.
54	3. **Then stop, and hand off in the open.** Open the PR with what is settled, name each unanswered
55	   question in the PR body under a heading that says the adoption is incomplete, and say the same
56	   on whatever issue prompted the run. Do **not** merge, do not proceed to a next pack's interview,
57	   and do not re-run the adoption on a later firing hoping the answer appeared — an unanswered
58	   question is a human's, and re-asking it weekly is nagging.
59	
60	A pack that asks nothing adopts fully unattended; this section costs it nothing.
61	
62	## 3. Re-vendor
63	
64	The new packs' prose, checks, and skills must land under the tracked `.claudinite/shared/` mount,
65	**and the repo must be stamped with the version it is now at.** Fetch a fresh canon to scratch and
66	run its install runner against the checkout — sessions never fetch:
67	
68	```
69	node <canon>/updates/install.mjs --target . <pack-id> [<pack-id>…]
70	```
71	
72	**Do not hand-roll this with `apply-vendor-set.mjs`.** It lays the files down correctly and does one
73	thing that nothing notices for weeks: it stamps **every declared pack** at the newest version,
74	whether or not the records between were ever applied. `migrationApplies` is `want > have`, so once
75	the stamp reaches a record's own version that record stops applying — not for this cycle, but
76	permanently. Re-vendoring a repo to add one pack therefore silently burns every pending record for
77	the packs it *already* had, and the repo is left claiming a version whose shape it was never
78	migrated into.
79	
80	That is correct behaviour at version zero, where there is no older state to skip; it is wrong
81	everywhere else, and adding a pack to a live repo is everywhere else.
82	
83	The runner declares each pack, vendors its content, stamps it and every pack in its `requires`
84	closure at the newest version, runs any one-shot seed ops, and gates on the converged tree's own
85	self-test. It exits non-zero on a refusal or an unanswered interview — a pack already installed is
86	**refused**, because reinstalling would restamp the repo to the newest version while skipping every
87	record in between.
88	
89	**Adopting `claudinite-tasks` also scaffolds the two workflow files** — the scheduler run with
90	its drain, and the label-event executor:
91	
92	```
93	node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/converge-workflows.mjs <owner/repo>
94	```
95	
96	`.github/workflows/` is the one directory a member's nightly may never push to, so these arrive
97	here or not at all. They are static from this moment: the cron minute is hashed from the repo's
98	full name, both anchor hours come from its `taskScheduler.dailyHour`, and every `run:` names a
99	mount path behind which the code converges nightly. The command is a no-op when both files are
100	already right. A repo adopting this pack also needs its two CCR routine endpoints — the executor's
101	and the work-item session's — pointed at `executor.md` and `queue/instructions.md` in its own
102	mount; that is a console setting, so it belongs in the handover issue §4b files.
103	
104	## 4. Scaffold what the pack now demands
105	
106	A newly active pack may require structure the repo doesn't have yet — deliberately, so the
107	declaration is a statement of intent that its own findings then guide you to satisfy. Run the
108	world sweep and let each finding name the file: e.g. `product-wiki` wants its index and the
109	reviewed `product-requirements/` sink before the isolation wall has anything to guard. Scaffold
110	per the pack's own README template; the pack's rules are the checklist.
111	
112	## 4b. File what adoption cannot do
113	
114	A pack may declare `adoptionHandover` — steps only a human can perform (a repository or
115	console setting, a permission, a secret). The install runner prints them; they are not
116	optional and they are not PR-body notes. **Open one tracking issue per adopting repo**,
117	a checkbox per step, written per
118	[writing-handover-issues](../../../basics/skills/writing-handover-issues/SKILL.md) — so
119	each step's `breaks` (what is broken while it is off) and `done` (its closing condition)
120	travel in the section below the checklist, never between the boxes. Per-repo manual work reliably does not happen,
121	so an unfiled step is a capability that dies silently in that member.
122	
123	Say on the adoption PR that the issue exists and link it. If the repo already has an
124	open issue for the same steps, comment there rather than opening a second.
125	
126	## 5. Land
127	
128	World and work checks green (`.claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs`; the Stop hook
129	carries the work checks). Commit referencing the task's issue, push, open one PR. Content a pack
130	seeds through this flow — a `product-wiki` wiki's first researched, cited pages — rides the same
131	review gate as any other change; it is never pushed straight to the default branch.
132	
133	**A failing check is your work, not the reviewer's.** Declaring a pack is what switched those rules
134	on, so every finding they now produce belongs to this change — fix it here, in the repo, before the
135	PR opens. Two things that are *not* fixes: silencing a rule by adding it to `rules`/`accept` in
136	`.claudinite-settings.json`, and undeclaring the pack to make the findings stop. Both turn a real
137	signal off on the repo's first exposure to it. If a finding genuinely cannot be satisfied — the pack
138	demands structure this repo has decided against — that is evidence the pack is **not** the right fit:
139	drop it from the declaration, say why on the PR, and let the smaller adoption land.
140	
141	**Never leave the repo red.** Whatever stops you — a check you cannot satisfy, an unanswered
142	interview question, a scaffold that needs a decision — get the tree green first and open the PR on
143	what is settled. An incomplete adoption in a green repo is a handoff; an incomplete adoption in a
144	red one is a bug report against you.
145

1	---
2	name: writing-claudinite-skills
3	description: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - "packs/*/skills/**"
7	---
8	
9	# Writing Claudinite skills
10	
11	A corpus skill is a harness-matched trigger (frontmatter `name` + a tight `description`, plus `force-load-on-file-edits-paths` under `metadata` where an edit of the files it names must not start without it — the PreToolUse guard holds such an edit until the skill is loaded; never the harness's `paths`, which limits when the skill is offered at all) plus the body the agent needs at usage time — well under 500 lines, and nothing a deterministic mechanism could carry instead (the promotion ladder in [engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md) decides). A skill may own the rules that validate its action — `checks.mjs` beside the SKILL.md, one module per rule, with their fixture tests under the owning pack's `test/` mirroring the skill's path; shape and the relevance-first gate in [engine/checks/README.md](../../../../engine/checks/README.md#adding-a-rule). Ownership is placement: the skill lives in exactly one owning pack's `skills/` — there is no skill catalog; the pack's own README names what it bundles. Instruction-writing *quality* — how agents actually follow docs — is [authoring-agent-docs](../../../basics/skills/authoring-agent-docs/SKILL.md)' turf; this skill is the corpus mechanics. (1)
12
