2	name: prose-to-checks
3	description: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
4	---
5	
6	# Convert existing prose to checks
7	
8	A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs: prose that is always-testable but was never converted
9	becomes a check, so the packs keep shedding context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is
10	first learned.
11	
12	## Two callers, differing only in scope
13	
14	- **The upgrade pass**, as the last step of a
15	  [growth-extract](../../tasks/growth-extract/task.md) run: the scope is the prose **that run just
16	  wrote**. Extraction already descends the promotion ladder per lesson, but a lesson written as prose
17	  under time pressure is exactly where a convertible rule hides, so it gets asked once more before the
18	  PR opens. Never widen from here into the standing backlog.
19	- **The weekly [prose-to-checks-sweep](../../tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)**: the scope is the
20	  **standing backlog** — everything under the pack paths configured for this repo, which the task
21	  passes in its Context. A consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by
22	  default — projects don't improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core
23	  `packs/`. Read the prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them).
24	
25	Plus on demand, when someone asks. Either way: never edit a read-only mounted canon pack under
26	`.claudinite/shared/`. Everything below is identical for both callers.
27	
28	## First gate — a working rule, not a product statement
29	
30	Before asking whether a rule is *testable*, ask whether it belongs to a pack at all: **does it govern
31	how we work, or state what the product does?** A pack — canon or local — homes the conventions,
32	gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks whatever the feature happens to be. A rule
33	asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or that a feature's parts are wired to
34	each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable spec and the suite that proves
35	it.
36	
37	This gate comes **first** because product statements sail through the check-the-world test below —
38	"this module must export `X`" has an obvious static signature. Converting one splits a feature's
39	definition across two systems and lands half of it in the one no test of the product ever reads.
40	Load-bearingness is not the test: a real gap in product coverage is a *requirements* gap. Neither is build
41	quality — a product statement converts into a genuinely well-made check, clean parse and see-it-fail proof and
42	all, and is still the wrong kind. The discriminator, applied **before** you write anything: *if the product
43	changed its mind tomorrow, would this rule be wrong?* Wrong → it's a requirement, and a red check would report
44	a product decision as a process violation. Still true whatever the product decides → it's a working rule.
45	
46	A product statement already sitting in pack prose is mis-homed, and a sweep is not the place to
47	re-home it. **Leave the prose and log it** as a mis-homed rule, the same way an un-checkable
48	candidate is logged — never cement it as a check.
49	
50	## Triage each candidate by where its signature lives
51	
52	Before asking whether a rule is checkable, ask where its violation would leave a mark, and route it
53	by that — a rule that reads as un-checkable is usually one whose mark is somewhere the check-the-world
54	question does not look:
55	
56	| The mark is in… | Class | Carrier |
57	|---|---|---|
58	| the tree, readable one file at a time | **A** | a declared world check, today's vocabulary |
59	| the tree, across files — a set derived first, then quantified | **B** | `extractValueSets` + `checkSetValues` / `checkSetPairs` / `requireIdenticalFiles` |
60	| the change — added or removed lines, a co-change, an untracked file, a reply class | **C** | a `scope: "work"` declaration |
61	| a tool call's input, before it runs | **D** | a `scope: "action"` declaration (`guardToolCalls`) |
62	| the session transcript — a reply's shape, a call sequence or count | **E** | a work rule over the transcript |
63	| nowhere, but the moment it applies is a tool call, a phrase, a path or a result | **F** | a skill with a `force-load-on-*` trigger |
64	| nowhere, and no moment to hang on | **G** | prose |
65	| a product statement or a platform setting | **H** | re-home; never convert |
66	
67	Record the class with the candidate. **A** and **B** go on to the check-the-world test below; **C** and
68	**D** convert straight into their scope's keys; **F** groups with every other rule sharing its trigger
69	into one skill, so a load carries the whole procedure; **G** stays.
70	
71	## What to look for — the check-the-world test
72	
73	For each rule that cleared the gate, ask the one question from
74	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
75	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
76	
77	- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
78	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
79	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
80	  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
81	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.
82	
83	**"Already covered by another check" is a claim to test, not to reason out** — hand the sibling check a file
84	that violates the rule before dropping the candidate as a duplicate. A ban list only covers the routes whoever
85	wrote it thought of, so the routes it misses are invisible to exactly the reasoning that drew it: three sweeps
86	running dropped an "the app opens no socket" rule because a neighbouring check banned the obvious networking
87	import, while the base library re-exported a raw socket call that sailed straight through.
88	
89	**"Not statically checkable" is a verdict about the tree's shape when it was taken, not about the rule —
90	re-derive it against today's sources.** A removal, a migration or a consolidation can collapse the entry points
91	a rule had to cover, and the objection dies with them: a "one deletable storage directory" rule needed
92	data-flow tracing while many entry points wrote paths, and needed none once one root remained. So when a sweep
93	meets prose an earlier sweep left behind, re-ask the question rather than trusting the recorded answer. (This
94	covers the *technical* verdict only — an owner's rejection of a conversion is settled.)
95	
96	**Read the conversion tracker's prior comments before authoring, not after.** Independent re-derivation is
97	exactly how duplicate work happens: a fresh reading of the same prose will happily re-nominate a rule, build it
98	out in full, and only then discover it was built and rejected before. The tracker is a precondition of the
99	work, not a place to log it — and record each rejection with its reason so the next run can act on it.
100	
101	**A static signature is necessary, not sufficient.** Both shapes the working-discipline rules bar
102	— a rule that pins today's code in place, and one derivable from the product's requirements —
103	answer *yes* here, so screen every candidate against that bar before converting it. Leave either
104	where it is; routing a requirement to the spec and its suite is its own change, not this sweep's.
105	
106	The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
107	part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.
108	
109	## How to convert one
110	
111	Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
112	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:
113	
114	> **The upgrade-pass caller lands inside growth-extract's own PR**, which auto-merges after CI — so the
115	> see-it-fail fixture is the only gate a converted check gets there. Convert only what you can prove;
116	> anything shakier stays prose and waits for the weekly sweep's reviewed PR.
117	
118	**A shape rule is a schema property, not a check.** Where the rule says a document must carry a field, take a
119	value from a closed set, have a type, or carry nothing beyond a key set, write it into the JSON Schema the
120	document points at with `$schema` — creating the schema on the first such rule — and let the
121	`schema-conformance` check enforce it; convert to a `checkParsedFiles` assertion only what a schema cannot
122	say (a relation between two documents, a value that depends on the tree). A declared assertion over a field
123	is a schema check in disguise, and a coded rule mirroring a schema's shape by hand is one that will drift.
124	
125	1. **Author the check** in the owning pack, at the ladder's highest check rung the rule allows: an entry
126	   in `<pack>/declared-checks.json` when its logic is patterns over files, dropping to `<pack>/<rule>.mjs`
127	   listed in `pack.mjs` only when it needs what patterns can't say. Either way the failure message *is*
128	   the rule (what / why / fix — plus, for a rule module, the `doc:` pointer back to the prose; a
129	   declaration carries no pointer and must state its own case).
130	2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
131	   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
132	   doesn't ship.
133	3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory when the rule is
134	   directional by kind, or when the condition is blocking-grade but **irreversible by the time it is
135	   observable** (an append-only transcript, a published artifact). A blocking finding no edit can
136	   retract never converges — it spends every remaining Stop cycle on something nothing can fix.
137	   Advisory there is *diagnostic*: it names the cause the moment it appears.
138	   - **Declare `since: '<today>'` beside the severity.** A blocking check is enforced as advisory for
139	     its first two weeks, so a conversion whose backlog the tree still carries lands at its real
140	     severity now and starts biting once somebody has had time to clear it. Never soften a real
141	     defect to `advisory` for that reason — the window is what makes softening unnecessary.
142	   - **Prefer a positive allowlist over an enumerated list of the bad cases.** Match the one allowed
143	     shape and flag everything else, rather than banning the violations you can name. An allowlist
144	     catches a variant that doesn't exist yet the day it lands, and turns an indirection (a value
145	     passed through a variable instead of written literally) into a finding too — refusing to reason
146	     about indirection is the feature. Invert only where the allowed set is genuinely open-ended.
147	4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
148	   how you decide which paragraphs those are.
149	
150	**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
151	its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
152	which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
153	*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
154	check to the same fixture bar.
155	
156	**When a rule mandates a *form*, the check asserts that form — never the intent behind it.** Where
157	the prose says *write it exactly like this*, the check's whole job is deciding whether the artifact
158	is that form; inferring what the author meant is unbounded in the wrong direction and leaves the
159	likeliest reproduction uncaught, since a hand-picked marker list always misses the phrasing nobody
160	enumerated. Expect a form check to fire on something that breaks the form while causing no harm —
161	that's the rule as written doing its job, not a reason to re-add intent-guessing.
162	
163	When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
164	candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.
165	
166	## Coming out: the deletion test
167	
168	Coming out of a conversion, apply the **deletion test**: prose a mechanism fully covers is
169	deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
170	paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent
171	how to fix it?* If yes, it is redundant: delete it whole. The check's failure message is where
172	the rule lives now and its header comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating
173	either pays twice and is the drift trap waiting to spring.
174	
175	Before concluding prose is the only carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an
176	activity-scoped skill often already holds the map a rule is repeating. Keep only what no artifact
177	carries.
178	
179	The test **discriminates** rather than just deleting: a paragraph stays whole whenever it carries
180	something the check does not — a second rule in the same breath, an exemption the check can't
181	encode, a value the check can't judge, or a remedy the finding's own `fix` line never states
182	(a finding renders `what` / `why` / `fix` / `doc`, never the rule's `description`, so a remedy
183	that lives only in the description is not carried). Two worked calls: an `npm test` invariant
184	went entirely — the check caught it and the testing-guide skill already listed the suites —
185	while an `extension-test/` mirror bullet stayed, because the check beside it enforced only the
186	`package.json` list's sync with the tree and never the mirror convention itself.
187	
188	Whether a check covers a rule is a judgment about meaning, so this test is applied by a
189	**reader**, not mechanized.
190	
191	## Bounds
192	
193	- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
194	  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
195	- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — the deletion test is only ever asked of a rule a
196	  *landed* check now enforces.
197	- Run the suite and the sweep green before the PR goes up, and never push to `main` directly. The
198	  sweep opens its own PR for the owner's approval; the upgrade pass adds its conversion to the
199	  growth-extract PR already being opened, and opens none of its own.
200

1	---
2	name: extract-from-activity
3	description: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from repo activity
7	
8	Mine what a window of work left behind — commits, the PRs merged in it, the issue discussion around
9	them — for durable, reusable lessons, and fold each into the repo's **own local packs**. Read only
10	what the work committed; the *dialogue* is [extract-from-conversations](../extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)'s.
11	
12	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
13	surface lives are shared with that sibling and stay canonical in
14	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't re-derive it. What follows is only
15	what reading *artifacts* adds.
16	
17	## Capture at the repo's own level
18	
19	Write each lesson at whatever level reads naturally for this repo — refer to its files, services, or
20	mechanics wherever that's what makes the lesson clear. Don't force either extreme: don't contort a lesson
21	to be hyper-specific, and don't polish it into a general, portable rule. Making a lesson portable is the
22	growth lifecycle's **promote** stage, done canon-side later over whatever merged here; here, just capture
23	it usefully and let promotion lift whatever turns out to travel.
24	
25	## Read the window — and read merged PRs properly
26	
27	Work only the window you were handed (a scheduled run gets it as binding scope in the work item's
28	Context; an owner's ask names it in words). Never widen it.
29	
30	1. **The commits** — full bodies, and the diff wherever a fix is non-obvious.
31	2. **The PRs merged in the window** — read these *first* and read them *whole*: the diff **and** the
32	   review discussion. A merged PR is usually the window's richest lesson source, because it records what
33	   was tried, what a reviewer pushed back on, and why the landed shape won. A verdict reached in review
34	   is a lesson already argued; the commit alone shows only the winner.
35	3. **The issue activity** it names — the comments changed on those numbers.
36	
37	## What artifacts signal — and what they don't
38	
39	The signals worth converting here are the ones an artifact can carry: a fix whose diff is small but whose
40	*reason* is not obvious from the code; a review comment that names a convention the author missed; a
41	revert or a follow-up fix that says the first shape was wrong; a PR that grew several rounds because its
42	approach was re-decided mid-flight.
43	
44	**An already-settled, already-enforced implementation choice is not a lesson.** If a check or a test
45	already pins the shape — which roots a CI sweep walks, which contract a construction must satisfy — and
46	all that is left to say is *why it looks like that*, it belongs at the implementation site rather than as
47	prose in a pack — and this run does not write there, so the candidate is dropped. A rule earns its place by
48	steering a **future** decision or catching a **repeatable** mistake, not by narrating a past one that is
49	already locked in.
50	
51	Wall-time and dialogue friction (a clarifying round-trip, a backtrack, a wait sat through) leave no trace
52	in a diff. Don't infer them from artifacts — that is the conversation sibling's territory, working from
53	logs that actually carry the timestamps.
54	
55	## Landing it
56	
57	Route each keeper down the ladder in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — a declared
58	check first, a custom code rule only where patterns can't say it, then pack skill, prose last — into the
59	local pack whose territory owns it. Write more checks and less prose, and keep each addition terse and in
60	the repo's own voice.
61	
62	A new check ships with its **red-first fixture**: see it fail on a violating fixture and pass on a clean
63	one. Declare `since: '<today>'` on it — a `blocking` check is enforced as advisory for its first two weeks,
64	so a check whose backlog the tree still carries can land now and bite later. A rule that cannot be made
65	confident lands as prose instead — never as a broken check.
66	
67	Finding nothing is a perfectly good and common outcome; a duplicate or invented "lesson" is worse than
68	adding nothing.
69

1	---
2	name: extract-from-conversations
3	description: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
4	---
5	
6	# Extract lessons from a conversation
7	
8	Read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions taken in it — and convert its friction into
9	changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer and less dependent on human steering. Read how the
10	work went; what the work committed is [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md)'s.
11	
12	The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
13	surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
14	re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.
15	
16	## The goal
17	
18	Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
19	waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
20	cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
21	a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.
22	
23	## Where the conversation comes from
24	
25	- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
26	  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
27	  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
28	  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
29	- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
30	  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.
31	
32	**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
33	when a session is done enough to mine.
34	
35	## What to look for — the friction signals
36	
37	Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
38	necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.
39	
40	### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user
41	
42	The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
43	building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
44	answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.
45	
46	**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
47	user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
48	a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
49	the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
50	correctly **without the round-trip**.
51	
52	### 2. Suboptimal agent actions
53	
54	The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
55	that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
56	something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
57	convention and had it corrected in review.
58	
59	**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
60	so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
61	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
62	first, not after a detour.
63	
64	### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them
65	
66	The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
67	padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
68	hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.
69	
70	**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
71	and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
72	(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
73	only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
74	was already optimal.
75	
76	**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
77	kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
78	the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
79	a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
80	loss of quality.
81	
82	## Encode the questions the user keeps asking
83	
84	The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
85	checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
86	fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
87	fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
88	relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
89	recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
90	retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.
91	
92	## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch
93	
94	Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:
95	
96	- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
97	- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
98	  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
99	  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
100	  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.
101	
102	The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
103	stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
104	every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
105	breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.
106	
107	## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it
108	
109	For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
110	(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
111	nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):
112	
113	- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
114	- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
115	  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.
116	
117	**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
118	beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
119	**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
120	deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
121	silence it replaced.
122

1	Below are rules on how to work on this repo.
2	
3	## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate
4	
5	- **Writing a `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md`** — the end state and its rationale only, with
6	  alternatives and their drawbacks. Never requests, prior-state narrative, or owner opinions.
7	
8	- **Recording a migration's plan, status or remaining work** — the tracking issue, never a
9	  `MIGRATION.md` beside the design (`writing-migration-plans`).
10	
11	- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` whose system is now built** — delete it whole rather than trim
12	  it. Verify each section already lives in a module header or pack `README.md` first, and move an
13	  owner-decision record with its rationale. Leave a doc describing work in flight alone. (4)
14	
15	- **Sweeping a deleted design doc's `§`-numbered pointers** — re-point each at a pack README, or
16	  drop it where the sentence only cited itself.
17	
18	- **Having a deferred direction, blocked proposal or status to record** — `docs/`, pointed at from
19	  the issue or PR. Never a pack file: `docs/` is outside the vendor set.
20	
21	- **Ending a session on unfinished work** — write the state into the tracking issue; the owner's
22	  opener is `continue work on #<n>`. Never compose a hand-off prompt.
23	
24	- **Wanting to verify or read something across members** — the executor's agent sessions are
25	  scoped to this repo alone, so a cross-repo `Verify:` parks on a scope denial minutes after
26	  being picked. The fleet half is a Shepherd fleet task, never an ad-hoc item here. (1)
27	
28	- **Designing anything that spans repos** — split it: a self-contained per-repo half in the canon,
29	  the aggregation half as a Shepherd fleet task. No repo list lives in canon code. (5)
30	
31	- **Landing a derived fleet artifact** — a daily auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file in Shepherd,
32	  never a commit to its `main`.
33	
34	- **Needing a member to flip a platform setting** — last resort; per-repo manual work reliably
35	  does not happen. Prefer the route that works with the Action's own `GITHUB_TOKEN`, or neutralise
36	  the blocking behaviour's effect rather than asking for a reconfiguration.
37	
38	- **Requiring a credential nothing weaker can replace** (`FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`) — name the exact
39	  scope, and have the automation report when it is missing rather than degrade silently.
40	
41	- **Landing a change to what members receive** — force delivery only where *"will it work on every
42	  repo?"* is live: engine flow, a contract member files must satisfy, a stub, a migration record, a
43	  new config key. Otherwise the nightly converge is the delivery. (6)
44	
45	- **Forcing fleet delivery** — drive Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` with `follow`, report per member
46	  unasked, and attach the repos verification needs. A dispatch is not a result; 204 means queued.
47	
48	- **Retiring a field, option or module** — `@deprecated` on its definition, plus a comment at each
49	  sanctioned holdout saying why it still carries the field. Never a bespoke conformance check for a
50	  deprecation; keep the contract validating it.
51	
52	- **Surfacing a number a human reads as a report card** — report a window against the previous
53	  window. Never a monotonic cumulative total, never a figure nothing measures. (9)
54	
55	- **Lacking a field a report-card number needs** — name it absent in the surface's own note. A
56	  stated gap is information, a guess is not. (10)
57	
58	- **Windowing a count** — only where it is built from things that happened inside the window. A
59	  figure derived from a point-in-time stamp reads a steady population as declining. (11)
60	
61	- **Classifying an open object by deriving it from other live state** — reconsider once the
62	  derivation's own inputs can mutate while the object stays open, silently reinterpreting its
63	  history. Prefer a marker stamped once at creation and never revisited.
64	
65	- **Scheduling the removal of a temporary compatibility tolerance** — gate it on a convergence
66	  window the change states for itself, never on a census of members: the canon cannot see which
67	  repos are active, inert or long stale, so "no member still stamps the old format" never reads
68	  true and the tolerance stands forever. (12)
69	
70	## Working with the owner and the session's tools
71	
72	- **Answering "why did it fail?"** — lead with the throwing call site: `file:line`, the function,
73	  and which side enforced it. A narrative that never names the line reads as unanswered.
74	
75	- **Reaching for `AskUserQuestion`** — it blocks ~170s, so spend it only on a fork you cannot take
76	  back. Anything answerable from the instruction, the tree, or a reversible default: answer it,
77	  act, and say what you assumed.
78	
79	- **Wanting to re-post a question the owner declined** — don't. Take its recommended default, or
80	  open the question up.
81	
82	- **Asking about a vague, destructive-sounding instruction** ("remove the entire mechanism") —
83	  scope the question to the boundary of the vague noun itself, not the consequences of one reading
84	  of it.
85	
86	- **Being asked to generalise something, or to review it** — land the conversions or action points
87	  it unlocks in the same change. A capability ships with its first caller, an analysis with its
88	  first recommendation applied.
89	
90	- **Calling anything on `Claude_Code_Remote`** — one call per intent, ever. Each costs minutes,
91	  and a call that returns nothing has not failed; the retry has run to 81% of a session's tool
92	  wall-clock.
93	
94	- **Wanting to read a public sibling repo** — `git clone --depth 1` (~2s). `add_repo` attaches
95	  nothing the git proxy does not already serve.
96	
97	- **Needing a session to read issues or PRs across several repos in one pass** — `add_repo`
98	  widens this session's own GitHub scope; unlike file content, issues aren't git refs, so there is
99	  no `git clone` substitute for reaching them.
100	
101	- **Waiting for something to happen** — the guard must name the condition awaited: a run's status,
102	  a file's arrival, a deadline. No trailing padded `sleep`. A guard you wouldn't write as the
103	  *whole* test means you are sleeping and calling it polling.
104	
105	- **Waiting on GitHub CI or PR check status** — read the head sha's check runs with the GitHub MCP
106	  tool, on a rolling backoff. This sandbox proxy-blocks `api.github.com`, so `Monitor` and shell
107	  poll loops report "still running" until they time out. (13)
108	
109	- **A `mcp__github__*` list/search/read call with no narrow `fields`/`per_page`** — risks a
110	  >25k-token single-line dump. The saved tool-result file is one unbroken line, so `Read`'s
111	  `offset`/`limit` won't shrink it; parse it with `python3 -c 'json.load(...)'` or `jq` instead.
112	
113	- **Re-waiting on a signal that already failed to move** — read the code that governs when it
114	  *can* change before waiting a second time on the same premise.
115	
116	- **Writing a step a human must do by hand into an issue** — make sure it is needed; a checklist
117	  of no-ops teaches the reader to skim it. Link the deepest existing settings URL rather than
118	  writing out a breadcrumb trail. (14)
119	
120	- **Replying to an owner comment that raises more than one claim** — answer every claim in that
121	  first reply, including the one you intend to push back on. (15)
122	
123	- **Repeating a design doc's stated architectural rationale** — verify each claimed ground against
124	  the current code first. "A task structurally cannot hold this permission" is false: code-work
125	  runs inside the executor's own Action job. (16)
126	
127	- **An owner reversing a standing decision** — purge every place in the repo that still states the
128	  old decision (docs, comments, code defaults) and record the new one where a future session reads
129	  it. Answering the prompting question alone is not the fix. (17)
130	
131	- **Sending a screenshot rendered from a scratch test harness** — say so in the caption, not just
132	  what the widget shows.
133	
134	- **Running a Bash command with a `cd` outside the project root** — the *next* Bash call silently
135	  resets cwd back to the root ("Shell cwd was reset to …"), whether the first command succeeded or
136	  failed. Prefix every command touching that directory with its own `cd`; a prior one never carries
137	  forward.
138	
139	- **Asserting why a system behaved a certain way** (a park correctly closed, a routing mechanism's
140	  logic) — read the primary evidence, the issue's own body/comments or the enforcing source line,
141	  first. A verdict inferred from structure or memory alone has shipped as a wrongly-merged fix for a
142	  bug that wasn't there.
143	
144	## Checks and capabilities built here
145	
146	- **Starting a new Claudinite-facing capability** — decide which distribution model it is before
147	  writing the first file: a member-local tool, always-on engine code, or an opt-in pack with its
148	  own adoption. Nothing prompts this choice, and getting it wrong costs a move-and-rewrite
149	  cycle. (19)
150	
151	- **Declaring a check, or adding a key to the vocabulary** — name the key so the declaration reads
152	  alone (`scanFiles`, `matchLines`, `relevantWhen`). If it needs a comment to be read, it needs a
153	  better name.
154	
155	- **Adding a legacy tolerance to `engine/` or `packs/`** — file the issue that removes it first,
156	  then put `// @legacy-tolerance advisory:<rule-id|none> retire:#<issue>` on the line directly
157	  above the declaration; `advisory:none` claims no member file can hold the old shape, so that
158	  issue must then name what does read the holder. (68)
159	
160	- **Creating the artifact a check will demand** — create it before the action it gates, not after.
161	
162	- **Changing a per-call hook** (`engine/hooks/*-judge.mjs`, the runner) — you are a guest in the
163	  harness: a judge returns a verdict and `hook-runner.mjs` alone exits, 0 or a deliberate 2;
164	  measure before and after with `node dev/tools/hook-latency.mjs` and record the numbers in the
165	  element's retrospective brief. (70)
166	
167	## The engine, the mount and what reaches members
168	
169	- **Editing `claudinite-scheduler.yml` or `claudinite-executor.yml`** — nothing beyond triggers,
170	  permissions, concurrency and the `run:` line naming an engine module. A converge cannot push to
171	  `.github/workflows/`, so logic left there costs a fleet-wide PR to change.
172	
173	- **Moving a scheduler workflow's program out** — into `packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/`, leaving a
174	  single-line `run: node <module>`, and edit both copies — the stub and the canon's own — in the
175	  same commit. `scheduler-workflows-are-thin` blocks the two shapes it can see.
176	
177	- **Writing a path, regex or command against the mount** — the two-root form: the
178	  `.claudinite/(shared|local)/` prefix optional in a pattern, and a probe for `.claudinite/shared/`
179	  falling back to the repo root. The home runs the same code from the repo root. (26)
180	
181	- **Tightening a contract member-owned files must satisfy** — first ask what carries it across the
182	  fleet. Vendoring refreshes `.claudinite/shared/` only and a migration record moves paths, not
183	  schemas; if nothing carries it, accept the legacy shape in `normalizeManifest`.
184	
185	- **Adding a key to the declared-check spec vocabulary** (`SPEC_KEYS` in `pattern-rules.mjs`) — an
186	  older engine drops that key and runs the rest of the declaration, so the new key buys nothing
187	  until its engine arrives. Write the declaration to be correct without it (#1400).
188	
189	- **A stale member declaration** — fail the run. Never let it degrade to *fewer checks running*.
190	
191	- **Renaming a pack whose config a member writes into their own repo** — a reader of that config
192	  resolves the new key and every legacy spelling, permanently. The rename map fixes code-side ids
193	  only; rewriting the write side reaches just the data the engine owns. (27)
194	
195	- **Checking whether an actor may trigger a privileged action off an issue/PR payload** — read
196	  `GET /repos/{o}/{r}/collaborators/{u}/permission`, never `author_association`: `MEMBER` covers
197	  any org member and `COLLABORATOR` includes read-only ones, both broader than push access. (28)
198	
199	- **Extending what a copied stub reads** — make the new config key optional, fail the run when it
200	  is declared-but-unset, and let declaring it trigger a staleness check. Stubs are copied once and
201	  never re-copied, so a new key is dead in every repo holding the old copy. (29)
202	
203	- **Writing a migration record that needs engine behaviour newer than itself** — have `appliesTo`
204	  probe the member's own mount for that capability by content, and stay inert until it reads back;
205	  an unreadable mount reads as "not capable". The executing worker is the member's vendored
206	  one. (30)
207	
208	- **Changing an export in `updates/*`** — empty it, never remove it, and say at its definition
209	  why. Fielded workers are stale callers of instantly-current flow modules, so a removal wedges
210	  every member permanently on its next run.
211	
212	- **Retiring an emptied `updates/*` export** — read the field: the condition is that no member's
213	  *vendored* worker calls it. Pin the surface with a test carrying an expiry; the canary rehearsal
214	  cannot catch this class.
215	
216	- **Renaming or deleting an `engine/` module a `packs/` file imports** — leave a shim at the old
217	  path re-exporting what it named. The two lanes deliver on separate cycles, so every member spends
218	  a window holding the NEW engine beside an OLD pack. (31)
219	
220	- **Asking which imported symbols are still fielded** — walk the TRUNK's pack history, never
221	  `--all`. An import that only ever existed on an unmerged branch is not fielded. (32)
222	
223	- **Changing a vendored stub** — edit the canon's own `.github/workflows/` copy in the same commit
224	  and diff the two whole files. The canon has no converge, so its copy drifts invisibly until it is
225	  a permission denial in production.
226	
227	- **Excluding files from the vendor set by pattern** — whitelist any operational file that matches
228	  by path, and pin it with a test against the real canon tree. The nightly refresh re-runs from
229	  canon HEAD, so a bug there is the one canon regression that is not self-healing. (33)
230	
231	- **Testing that an operational file still vendors** — assert the whole containing directory, not
232	  the one file that broke; otherwise the next file added there needs a fresh edit. (34)
233	
234	- **Retiring or reshaping a protocol the engine exposes** — sweep for callers outside this repo,
235	  not just what greps locally. Two stub copies at the same path declaring different input names is
236	  the same failure from the other side: the two spellings *are* the protocol. (35)
237	
238	- **Branching on the result of an API write in fleet machinery** — read its status, not just the
239	  body. A body-only destructure turns a 403 into a plausible object and the run still logs `ok`.
240	
241	- **Judging whether fleet delivery worked** — members' stamps, never run conclusions. The stamp is
242	  the only artifact that moves.
243	
244	- **A single timeout bound covering two different waits** ("has this started" vs "is something
245	  already running about to finish") — split it, sized from each phase's own declared budget rather
246	  than a round number. (36)
247	
248	- **Writing a give-up message for a hit timeout** — say it is a statement about the clock, not a
249	  verdict on the work. "No successful run yet" sends a reader chasing a settings diagnosis for CI
250	  that was simply still running. (37)
251	
252	- **Writing generated content into a size-capped GitHub API field** — budget it in two tiers: an
253	  always-complete compact summary, plus best-effort detail rationed to a byte budget with an
254	  explicit omitted-count. An unbounded write 422s at the ~64KB cap. (38)
255	
256	- **Writing a generated title whose content scales with a list** — collapse the list to a count
257	  and keep per-item detail in the body. A title is a summary surface, not a second body.
258	
259	- **Preflighting a required grant or permission** — a probe run where the failure's condition
260	  isn't met reports a false-positive pass. Prefer attributing a real observed 403 to the
261	  permission that would fix it. (39)
262	
263	- **Introducing a finer-grained classification of a catch-all state** — default whatever an older
264	  or unaware writer produces to the most conservative member of the new set, so it fails safe
265	  instead of landing in a lane nobody watches.
266	
267	- **Adding a fleet task** — fail loudly on a Context target it cannot reach rather than proceeding
268	  on a partial list, and treat a member as un-adopted until the routine's repo scope names it.
269	  Otherwise the drift completes, filing a report that reads as a full sweep. (40)
270	
271	- **Spawning a child process from a worker** — pass an explicit `cwd`, resolved to a root that
272	  cannot vanish (`--root`, then `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, then `cwd`). The converge deletes the tree
273	  its own code-work runs inside.
274	
275	- **A worker crash sharing a benign outcome code** — keep "could not run" distinguishable from
276	  "had nothing to run", or it is unobservable.
277	
278	- **Diagnosing a member's maintenance PR that won't land** — `unstable` beside a green sweep is a
279	  parked `action_required` run, not a missing repo setting.
280	
281	- **Reading a uniform signal across every fleet member** — check for a rate-limit signal before
282	  trusting a uniform empty sweep, and check whether each member's own convergence window has passed
283	  before calling the fleet frozen.
284	
285	- **Corroborating a theory with a signal already known unreliable** — don't. An uncorrected "the
286	  entire fleet is frozen" claim stood for ~10 hours.
287	
288	- **Retiring or migrating a dispatch/config parameter channel** — a parameter that stops being
289	  read must fail loudly, never silently default. A dropped safety knob (`DRY_RUN`) defaults to the
290	  operation's most dangerous mode. (41)
291	
292	- **Relying on a push to trigger further Actions workflows** — a push authored with the default
293	  `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which every converge and auto-merge here uses, fires no `on: push` workflow. Only
294	  a real user or app credential cascades. (42)
295	
296	- **A workflow file referencing a renamed entry point by literal path** — hold a shim open, as for
297	  an `engine/` module a `packs/` file imports. `.github/workflows/` lands only through a PR a human
298	  merges. (43)
299	
300	- **A script written for one execution context** — audit every script's environment assumptions (a
301	  real `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `gh`/`curl` reachability) whenever its caller's context changes. Every
302	  script built against the old assumption fails identically, not just the one that broke first.
303	
304	- **Picking a compact date-encoded identifier** — check the encoding's rollover boundary years
305	  ahead, not just today's decode. Anchoring a year on its last digit wraps to 0 in 2030; use
306	  `year - 2020`, not `year % 10`. (45)
307	
308	- **Carrying a dotted version identifier** — keep it string-typed everywhere. `'60820.10'` and
309	  `'60820.1'` are different versions and the same float. (46)
310	
311	- **Designing text that instructs a model to echo an exact string** — state the instruction first,
312	  have it disclaim itself as instruction-not-payload, and put the literal string once, last. Never
313	  reference the payload anaphorically ("that line"); recency is what resolves it. (47)
314	
315	## Scheduled tasks
316	
317	- **Filing an issue no person will ever act on** — a board, a watermark, the machine's own
318	  bookkeeping — file it CLOSED and labelled, state both on every write so a reopened or
319	  pre-rule one converges, and find it by that label rather than paging the repo's closed
320	  history. (69)
321	
322	- **Opening a queue work-item's own delivered PR** — never `Closes #<the item's own issue>` in
323	  the body. `converge-item.mjs` closes or parks that issue with the right label state; the native
324	  keyword fires on merge regardless and overrides an intended `needs-human-approval` park. (49)
325	
326	- **Choosing a task's cadence** — take it from how often the signal actually moves. A weekly run
327	  still sees all 7 days, because a task's signal window is its own period plus an hour of slack.
328	
329	- **A precondition that fires nearly every night** (one reading `sharedMount`) — daily buys noise,
330	  not freshness, and spends an opus session each time. Prefer weekly where the work isn't
331	  latency-sensitive.
332	
333	- **After any scheduler-mechanism flip** — re-audit every task whose precondition assumed the old
334	  mechanism; grep for `frequency: 'manual'` plus its precondition text, not just the flipped
335	  mechanism's callers. A stale `run: false` becomes a live self-closing landmine. (50)
336	
337	- **Writing a task's precondition** — gate on the objects' own movement in the window (a `touched`
338	  list, a tip-commit date), never on standing state, which is true forever once true. (portable →
339	  `claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md`)
340	
341	- **A precondition signal that is true most days** — let it only *widen* an already-triggered run.
342	
343	- **Scoping a task whose verdict is relative to the rest of a set** — the gate is not the scope:
344	  newness gates, and the full set stays the scope.
345	
346	- **Writing a task whose output is a regenerated file** — land it through
347	  `packs/claudinite-tasks/deliver-generated.mjs`, reading prior state from the fetched base, not local
348	  HEAD. (`basics/baselining` is the deliberate exception.)
349	
350	- **A worker that checks out a branch or leaves an index behind** — one executor run drains
351	  several items from one checkout, so it hands the next item a tree it did not expect.
352	
353	- **Wanting to exercise a task Action-side** — dispatch the scheduler workflow with its `wake`
354	  input naming the task; the post-scheduler drain picks it up in the same run. The precondition
355	  still runs at pickup, so a wake that finds no work says so — a verdict, not a failure.
356	
357	- **Converging an unattended run** — do the label/comment/close sequence as the run's very next
358	  action once the outcome is known, never deferred to a checklist recalled at the end of a long
359	  session. (51)
360	
361	- **Closing a run `outcome:done`** — it means nothing is left for anyone to act on. Never while a
362	  PR, branch, or open question from this run is still live.
363	
364	- **Decomposing a pipeline into chained tasks** — chain stages by preconditions that each
365	  re-derive the world's actual state, never by parameters passed forward. A run interrupted
366	  mid-pipeline then self-heals on the next pick.
367	
368	- **Setting `on_interrupt: 'needs-human'`** — narrow it to the one stage whose side effect is
369	  genuinely non-idempotent. (52)
370	
371	- **Passing a diagnostic verdict out of a subprocess that may be killed at its timeout ceiling** —
372	  write it to stdout/stderr, never a file written at exit. Already-printed output survives a
373	  `SIGKILL`. (53)
374	
375	- **Writing a repair rule over a live, mutating collection** — a rule gated on *current state*
376	  needs a fresh, targeted read of the item immediately before acting, never the snapshot that
377	  triggered the sweep. A rule gated on a *clock* is safe against snapshot staleness.
378	
379	- **Solving a "must act again later" problem** — check whether an existing generic lane already
380	  carries it before building standing machinery. The deferred-request queue's
381	  `Blocked-by`/`Not-before` lane does.
382	
383	- **Building a dedup or mutex over work items** — key the guard on the target the write lands on,
384	  never the requester's phrasing. A same-title match is blind to two items writing one target under
385	  different titles; `Blocked-by:` is what serializes them. (54)
386	
387	- **Converging a work item from a session** — `converge-item.mjs` prints the calls; making them
388	  verbatim with your own GitHub tools is the whole path, on every session, with or without a REST
389	  route. Hand-fabricating the transition is how an item ends up closed wearing a live status, or
390	  labelled `done` and left open. (2)
391	
392	## Proving a change
393	
394	- **Testing a change to a task's triggering** — drive the real `planSchedulerRun` from a clock at
395	  which the task's anchor has NOT come. Instantiation is decided before any precondition runs, so
396	  starting from a queued item proves only "works once instantiated".
397	
398	- **Testing a fail-soft step** — assert the positive effect (the output IS emitted), never
399	  `status === 0`, which fail-soft makes meaningless. The engine is vendored verbatim, so one
400	  regression disables that step fleet-wide.
401	
402	- **Testing a helper reapplied across a hand-off, a re-queue or a retry** — call it twice and
403	  assert no duplication. A suite of single-call tests stays green while the multi-call case
404	  corrupts state.
405	
406	- **Testing a mechanism that arbitrates by identity** (a claim, a lock) — the second call must
407	  come from a *different actor*. One actor retrying its own stale claim can't expose an
408	  identity-masked race. (55)
409	
410	- **Building a simulator for a stateful engine mechanism** — model what the engine's code actually
411	  *writes*, never the rule's stated *intent*. A sim advancing state wherever the rule's description
412	  matches is correct by construction and blind to where the two diverge.
413	
414	- **Asserting a mid-run invariant** — capture it at the exact moment the state holds. By the end
415	  of the run, normal convergence has cleared the evidence.
416	
417	- **Writing a regression test that pins a policy or convention decision** — assert the
418	  behavior/invariant the decision requires, never a literal sentence quoted from a doc: a
419	  sentence-matching test stays green even while a sibling doc states the opposite, certifying the
420	  contradiction instead of catching it.
421	
422	- **A test that derives its answer by walking git history** — guard explicitly against a shallow
423	  clone and fail loudly. It otherwise passes vacuously exactly when the real answer needs history
424	  it doesn't have. (56)
425	
426	- **Restoring source after a deliberate see-it-fail mutation** — `git checkout -- <file>` at the
427	  moment of mutating, never a `.bak` taken earlier, which predates whatever else you edited in
428	  between. (57)
429	
430	- **Mutating a file to see a check fail** — commit or stage the real edit first, and only mutate a
431	  file whose current state you are ready to throw away. `git checkout --` restores from the index,
432	  destroying uncommitted work just as thoroughly. (58)
433	
434	- **Surveying whether something exists in the tree** — a code-search hit is evidence; a miss is
435	  not. Survey by reading each file.
436	
437	- **Documenting or relying on a named knob** — grep for the code that reads it and the code that
438	  writes it first. The corpus naming it is not evidence it exists; all three misses are real
439	  here. (62)
440	
441	- **Deleting a writer** — it is the same change as marking its series historical. Its rows keep
442	  counting plausibly until the retention window ages out, then count nothing. (63)
443	
444	- **Renaming an entity** — sweep for references in code and comments, don't change historical
445	  records, and re-render generated files rather than editing them by hand.
446	
447	- **Sweeping a rename mid-migration across many PRs** — a file added or rewritten after the sweep
448	  starts can independently reinvent the retired constant as a comparison key; a state comparison
449	  against it fails silently, with no error and no failing test, only a wrong count. (3)
450	
451	- **Renaming a word that is also stored data** (a counter key, a wire word, a label) — rename it
452	  on the **decode** side too, or the next encode writes those historical counts as `null`,
453	  silently and only for the old rows.
454	
455	- **A second rename of one name** — map every legacy spelling straight to today's, never chaining
456	  one normalization onto the last, so the oldest vocabulary still normalizes in a single pass. (64)
457	
458	- **Writing a "this period is covered" marker in an idempotent pipeline** — write it strictly
459	  after the durable effect it guards, and scope it to the *declined* case only. A go verdict's
460	  coverage is judged by the item it created, never by the row.
461	
462	- **Verifying a bulk file-move or rewrite sweep preserved content** — check a structural invariant
463	  count before and after (total `test(` calls across the touched files). One sweep truncated 46
464	  test files to zero bytes and every one still "passed".
465	
466	## Editing, branching and merging here
467	
468	- **Making a throwaway probe commit on a scratch branch** — `git commit -am` stages every modified
469	  file, and a later `git branch -D` discards the real in-progress edits it swept up. Isolate
470	  pending edits first.
471	
472	- **Editing a repo's JSON config** — patch it as anchored text; never re-serialize. A round-trip
473	  rewrites indent, key order and escapes while nothing fails and tests stay green. (portable →
474	  `repo-text-sweeps`)
475	
476	- **A JSON target nested inside an array within an entry object** — parse and rewrite
477	  structurally, preserving key order and `via`/`config`/answers by hand. An anchored regex cannot
478	  cross the nested closing bracket, and a fixture without that nesting proves nothing. (65)
479	
480	- **Returning to a branch that waited** — after `git fetch`, re-verify the *premise* unasked: say
481	  whether the problem is still there and what survives. This repo auto-merges its own PRs on top of
482	  migrations that retire whole directories.
483	
484	- **Re-verifying a branch against a `main` that has moved** — `git rebase origin/main`, never
485	  `git merge origin/main`. A merge commit trips the blocking squash-merge-history check. (66)
486	
487	- **Merging a PR that has sat open across many `main` commits** — check its current
488	  `mergeable_state`, not an old green CI run. A structural change on `main` since (a directory
489	  move, a renamed path) can turn a once-clean branch conflicted without a new run ever failing.
490	
491	- **After a PR lands by squash-merge** — `git remote prune origin` before touching that branch
492	  again. GitHub deletes the head ref here, so a stale tracking ref makes the next push reject and
493	  the stop hook report phantom local work. (67)
494	
495	- **Re-applying your edit onto a moved `main`** — re-read the fetched file, apply the same
496	  anchored edit, and confirm the stat shows insertions only. A pack's `RULES.md` is append-only
497	  and written several times a day, so a whole-file copy deletes those lessons and nothing goes
498	  red.
499	
500	- **Syncing local `main`** — `git fetch origin main && git reset --hard origin/main`,
501	  unconditionally. The clones are shallow, so `git pull` finds no common ancestor; nothing of value
502	  is ever on this repo's local `main`. (portable → `git-github`)
503	
504	- **Merging in a session that also has a consumer repo in its sources** — resolve the merge skill
505	  by *target repo*, not by which matched first. The consumer's wins on name, silently skipping the
506	  canon-only post-merge conversation capture
507	  (`node packs/claudinite-growth/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), which is part of the merge.
508	
509	- **Having work that completes or corrects an open PR** — put it on that PR's branch. A dispatch
510	  prompt's designated branch routes work, not review; splitting gives the owner two gates for one
511	  decision.
512	
513	- **Wanting to combine two PRs** — update the one you're keeping and close the other. Never push
514	  one's branch onto the other's base: GitHub marks a PR merged once its head is reachable, and a
515	  later `state: closed` is a no-op. Check the API's `merged` field before reporting.
516	
517	- **Being asked "should no X decide this?"** — it questions whether the decision exists at all;
518	  never answer by relocating the knob one rung out. Ask who would set it differently and why that
519	  can't be read off the structure.
520	
521	- **Facing a retry across a call whose outcome you cannot observe** — check whether declining to
522	  retry removes the uncertainty before building dedup machinery to manage it.
523	
524	- **Writing a regex import-path rewriter for a bulk file-move** — anchor to real import/export
525	  syntax (line-start, or after a specific separator), never a bare `from '...'` searched across the
526	  whole text. A fixture embedding import syntax as string data matches identically and is corrupted.
527	
528	- **Running the prose-to-checks sweep here** — the worklist is
529	  `docs/declarative-checks/rule-inventory.md`, every rule classified by the moment that could
530	  carry it; convert from its A–F rows, and correct a mis-read row there, dated, rather than
531	  re-deriving the class.
532
