1	---
2	name: google-id-token-validation
3	description: Wiring server-side validation of Google Sign-In ID tokens — a JWT authorizer or OIDC verifier — and handling their claims. Use when adding or changing such validation.
4	---
5	
6	# Google ID-token validation
7	
8	Wire the validator however the project dictates (an API Gateway JWT authorizer, a `jose`/`jsonwebtoken` verifier, a Cloud Function). Acquiring the token client-side is out of scope.
9

1	---
2	name: jwt-minting
3	description: Issuing or signing JWTs — choosing the algorithm, generating keys, deciding the claims. Use when adding or changing code that creates tokens.
4	---
5	
6	# JWT minting
7	
8	- **Algorithm by trust shape.** HS256 only when signer and verifier are the *same party* — anyone who can verify an HMAC token can also mint one. One-to-many (APIs, federated identity) → RS256/ES256 (ES256: same strength, smaller keys and signatures).
9	- **Keys.** From a CSPRNG, never a password: an HMAC secret must be ≥ 256 random bits (32+ chars — RFC 7518 requires at least the hash-output length, and short/guessable secrets are practically brute-forceable). Asymmetric pairs:
10	  - RSA: `openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -out private.pem -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:2048`
11	  - EC P-256: `openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey -noout -out ec_private.pem`
12	
13	  Load key material from the environment or a secret store — never source. Use a **different key per subsystem/token type**; one shared key is what makes cross-service substitution possible.
14	- **Claims.** Always set `sub`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp` — and make `iss`/`aud` specific (the subsystem's URL, not the company name) so exact-match validation has something to bite on. Keep `exp` short; long-lived access rides a refresh token, not a long expiry. Use `typ` to separate application token types.
15	- **Payload is readable by anyone** — Base64 is encoding, not encryption. No secrets or private data in a signed-only token; use JWE when third parties must not read it, and in multi-party flows **sign first, then encrypt** the signed token.
16	- **Client-side sessions are still client data.** Size the token (every request carries it), store it `HttpOnly` when cookied, and pair with CSRF mitigations — a stolen token *is* the session.
17

1	---
2	name: jwt-validation
3	description: Wiring or changing JWT verification — pinning algorithms, validating claims, nested or encrypted tokens. Use when adding or changing code that accepts JWTs.
4	---
5	
6	# JWT validation
7	
8	A token is valid only when the signature **and** every claim you rely on check out. The bundled checks enforce the static half (no `alg: none`, pinned algorithms, audience binding, no literal secrets); the judgment half:
9	
10	- **You pick the algorithm, never the token.** Configure the verifier with the exact algorithm(s) you issue and reject everything else — the attacker writes the header, so branching on its `alg` hands them the choice (`none`, or HS256 keyed with your published RSA public key).
11	- **Match key type to algorithm family.** An HMAC secret belongs only to HS\*, a public key object only to RS/ES/PS\*. A verify API taking one string-or-key argument is where the RS256-public-key-as-HS256-secret forgery lives — prefer APIs (or key objects) that separate the two.
12	- **Validate every claim present**: `exp`/`nbf` (allow a small clock skew), and `iss`/`aud` by **exact match** — a substring or prefix check re-opens substitution between services sharing a key.
13	- **`decode()` is not `verify()`.** A decode-only helper is for display; nothing read from it may drive authorization.
14	- **Nested JWTs: validate every layer.** Decrypting an outer JWE never vouches for the inner JWS — verify the inner signature too (`cty: JWT` marks the nesting).
15	- **JWE is not authenticity when producer ≠ consumer.** Anyone holding the public key can mint a validly-encrypted token; the auth tag only proves ciphertext integrity. Multi-party flows need a nested signed JWT — signed first, then encrypted.
16	- **One validation rule-set per token type.** Distinct `typ` values (JWS allows application-specific ones), distinct keys per subsystem, per-type claim checks — so an access token can never pass where a session-cart token is expected.
17

1	# Headless browser
2	
3	## Getting a browser
4	
5	- **Resolve the binary out of the environment; never let the driver download one.** A container
6	  or runner image that already ships a browser is the normal case, and the driver's own registry
7	  download is slow, often blocked, and pins a build you did not choose. Look for an explicit
8	  override variable first, then the image's browser root, then fall through to the driver's own
9	  resolution — and prefer the driver's `-core` package, which bundles no browser at all. The
10	  image's build number need not match the driver's own pin for the browser to launch. Never
11	  hardcode the version-stamped path you found by looking: it moves with the next image, and the
12	  failure lands on whoever rebuilds rather than on whoever wrote it.
13	
14	- **A fresh install of the driver package is the same danger from upstream.** Reinstalling the
15	  package to fix an import error just as easily resolves to a newer release than the one paired
16	  with the environment's pinned browser — it then hunts for a browser build the image was never
17	  given and fails asking for a network install the sandbox cannot make. A reinstall run from the
18	  repo root instead of a scratchpad can dodge that failure outright (a version happens to
19	  resolve that works) and still cost you: it dirties the tracked `package.json`, its lockfile and
20	  `node_modules`, which then need a manual revert before anything can be committed. Resolve the
21	  already-installed package by its global path instead of adding a second copy, at any depth in
22	  the tree.
23	
24	- **When a page depends on a third-party library loaded from a CDN you have not vendored,
25	  stub the library's own API surface rather than trying to make the CDN reachable.** A default
26	  network abort (above) leaves the page's global for that library undefined, so every call into
27	  it throws and the render comes back empty — indistinguishable from a product bug unless you
28	  know the cause. Grep the code under test for the handful of calls it actually makes (a mapping
29	  or charting library often boils down to a handful of constructors and methods) and install a
30	  minimal no-op implementation of just those as an init script, before the page's own scripts run.
31	
32	- **A committed pixel golden is only comparable under the exact build that rendered it.** Two
33	  browsers a version apart rasterise text and shadows differently, so a comparison across them
34	  measures the renderer, not the product. Where the output is compared pixel by pixel, read the
35	  installed driver version at launch and **refuse to run** on any other, naming the pinned one in
36	  the error; where it is not — a build artifact, a behavioural assertion — let the build float
37	  and spend nothing on pinning it.
38	
39	- **Pinning is what buys a zero-diff browser golden — budget for the whole recipe or accept a
40	  tolerance.** A browser screenshot is not bit-stable across machines by default, which is why
41	  the general advice is a small tolerance. It *can* be made bit-stable, and the price is this
42	  pack's next two sections in full: the pinned build, a font jail, and the rasterisation flags.
43	  Take all of it or take the tolerance; a half-applied recipe gives a zero-diff gate that fails
44	  on someone else's machine for reasons no one can read off the diff.
45	
46	## The page's world is an input — replace all of it
47	
48	- **Serve the page from a fake origin you fulfil from disk, and abort anything you did not
49	  name.** Intercepting at the browser needs no server process, no port and no free-port race,
50	  and it reaches *every* request the page makes rather than the ones an application-level mock
51	  happens to know about. Make the default arm an abort: a new external dependency then breaks
52	  the run loudly instead of quietly adding real network to a run meant to be hermetic.
53	
54	- **Use an `https` fake origin.** Geolocation and several other capabilities exist only on a
55	  secure origin, and a page served over `http` silently takes the denied path instead. Routes
56	  are fulfilled before any connection is attempted, so no certificate is involved and nothing
57	  has to be trusted.
58	
59	- **Route a vendored third-party asset host-agnostically.** A stylesheet you serve in place of a
60	  CDN copy still resolves *its own* relative URLs against the host it was served from, so the
61	  font or image files it references arrive addressed to that CDN. Match those follow-up requests
62	  on the path alone, on any host, or the sheet loads and every asset it names 404s — which
63	  renders as a silent fallback rather than an error.
64	
65	- **Know which knobs are fixed at context creation and which are per page.** Locale, timezone,
66	  viewport, device scale factor, geolocation and permissions belong to the browser *context* and
67	  cannot be changed once it exists — so proving that a product reads a fixed zone rather than
68	  the device's takes **two** contexts, not one page reconfigured twice. The clock, seeded
69	  randomness and injected scripts are per page.
70	
71	- **A command-line window-size flag is not a viewport — a narrow one does not test the narrow
72	  layout.** Ask a browser's *CLI* for a phone-sized window and it renders the page at a clamped
73	  width and crops the overflow, without applying the media queries the width should have
74	  triggered. The output looks exactly like a horizontal-overflow bug in every section of a page
75	  that has none, and the instinct is to go hunting through the CSS for the offender. Only a
76	  context or page created with an explicit viewport puts the page in that layout. Reserve the
77	  CLI screenshot for the width the window happens to be, and give it a virtual-time budget that
78	  outlasts the page's entrance animations, or sections capture mid-transition and read as broken
79	  when they are fine.
80	
81	- **Install every fake as an init script, so it runs before the page's first script.** A stub
82	  installed after load has already lost every call made during boot. Seeded randomness, storage
83	  seeds, and any API you are replacing all belong there.
84	
85	- **Freezing CSS animation does not freeze the Web Animations API.** Zeroing
86	  `animation-duration` and `transition-duration` stops declarative animation and nothing else;
87	  anything driven through `element.animate` keeps running, and a capture races it. Stub the
88	  method so every such animation resolves on its end state immediately.
89	
90	- **Give the clock two modes and pick deliberately.** A fixed instant is right for a resting
91	  state. A requirement about what the *passage* of time changes needs the clock installed and
92	  paused instead, so the page's timers exist and can be wound forward on purpose — a fixed clock
93	  has no timers to advance.
94	
95	## Fonts decide the layout, and the machine decides the fonts
96	
97	- **Vendoring the web fonts is half the job — every glyph they lack is drawn from the machine.**
98	  An emoji, an arrow, a currency sign, a non-Latin title: each falls back to whatever the host
99	  has installed, so the rendering quietly becomes a record of that machine's font set. The
100	  failure is brutal and unobvious — one string measures wider on a runner than on a workstation,
101	  wraps, and every card below it moves down a line. Launch the browser with its own
102	  font-configuration world whose only font directory is one you vendored, with the generic
103	  families aliased into it, so nothing installed on the host can reach the page.
104	
105	- **Ask the browser for reproducible rasterisation.** Disable hinting and subpixel text, force
106	  an sRGB colour profile, hide scrollbars, and disable GPU rasterisation. Shadows and blurs need
107	  two more: partial raster reuses tiles whose seams land inside a blur, and runtime-optimised
108	  drawing routines differ by CPU — both make the *same* page render differently run to run on
109	  one machine.
110	
111	## Capturing
112	
113	- **Wait on something the page itself produces, never on the network going quiet.** A selector
114	  that only exists once data rendered, or text that only appears once an async read returned, is
115	  a real signal; "no requests for a moment" is a guess that is wrong in both directions. Await
116	  font readiness too — text laid out before the fonts land is a different image.
117	
118	- **Clip at an element's box rather than screenshotting the element.** An element screenshot
119	  scrolls the element into view first, and a scroll dismisses whatever hover or focus opened the
120	  state you came to capture. A clip moves nothing. For the same reason, open hover-driven UI at
121	  capture time rather than in a preceding drive step, and settle the scroll position
122	  deliberately before measuring anything.
123	
124	- **A bounding box is viewport-space and goes stale.** Drivers scroll an element into view
125	  before clicking it, so a rectangle measured before a click means somewhere else after one.
126	  Convert to document coordinates at the moment of measurement, then take the clip from a
127	  full-page shot so a region below the fold is still inside the rendered image.
128	
129	- **Round a clip to whole pixels.** A layout rectangle is fractional; letting a fractional clip
130	  reach the screenshot leaves the rounding to the renderer, and half a pixel either way is a
131	  different image. Clamp it to the page's own bounds as well — a clip outside the rendered image
132	  is an error, not a crop.
133	
134	- **Rendering a shipped page outside its runtime means removing the scripts that need that
135	  runtime.** They throw on the first missing global and populate nothing, so the capture is of
136	  an empty surface that looks like a product bug. Strip them after load and set the state you
137	  meant to show yourself.
138	
139	- **Launch once and reuse the browser across captures.** Process startup dominates the cost of a
140	  capture, so a fresh browser per shot turns a fast run into a slow one for nothing; take a new
141	  context or page per capture instead, and close it, so no state leaks between them.
142

1	# Flutter
2	
3	## Architecture: ports out of the widget tree
4	
5	- **Widgets depend on ports, never on plugins.** Every platform/backend concern (location, auth,
6	  push, backend calls, the clock) enters the UI as a hand-written abstract interface with pure-Dart
7	  value types; plugin adapters (`geolocator`, `firebase_*`, `google_sign_in`, …) implement them and
8	  are constructed **only** in `main.dart`. A plugin type leaking into a screen (a geolocator
9	  `Position`, a `FirebaseFunctionsException`) is a defect: it silently couples every widget test to
10	  the plugin's platform channels.
11	- **Enforce the boundary with a committed import-scan test** (dart:io over `lib/ui/`, `lib/screens/`
12	  looking for forbidden import prefixes). The analyzer won't stop a convenient leak.
13	- **Ship the fakes in the package** (`lib/testing/`): scripted fakes for each port that also
14	  *record* what the UI asked of them, plus a `FakeWorld` bundling them with a pinned clock and the
15	  real app shell. Both the app's own tests and any sibling test package (e.g. an
16	  executable-requirements suite) import one fake world — never two parallel ones.
17	- **Extract the root shell into a widget** (`lib/app.dart`) taking the ports as parameters, used
18	  identically by `main.dart` (adapters) and the test harness (fakes). Tests must never rebuild a
19	  parallel MaterialApp — actuals come from the shipped shell.
20	- **Inject the clock.** Any widget that formats or compares times takes a `Clock` port; relative
21	  time rendered from `DateTime.now()` is untestable and drifts goldens.
22	
23	## Widget tests and goldens
24	
25	- **Anything that fetches must be injectable**: map tile providers, avatar images. Widget tests
26	  block real HTTP (a 400-returning stub client), so a `NetworkImage`/network `TileProvider` in the
27	  tree means error boxes, not screenshots. Provide a deterministic in-memory substitute (a
28	  canvas-drawn `ImageProvider` works and needs no asset files).
29	- **Async lifecycle guards need an epoch counter.** A `start()` that awaits (permission check,
30	  first fix) can re-arm streams/timers after `stop()`/dispose ran mid-await; bump an epoch in
31	  `stop()` and bail after every await if it changed. The symptom (leaked GPS subscription after
32	  sign-out) is invisible in tests that don't await realistically.
33	
34	## Toolchain habits
35	
36	- **Verify plugin APIs against the installed source, not memory.** Major Flutter plugins break
37	  their APIs often (google_sign_in v7's `authenticate()`, flutter_map v7+'s options, geolocator's
38	  settings objects); resolved versions live in the pub cache
39	  (`~/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/<pkg>-<ver>/lib/`) — read them before writing against them.
40	- **`flutter analyze` at zero issues** (infos included) is the bar a suite holds; lints that fight
41	  a deliberate convention (e.g. `file_names` vs. leaf-id case filenames) get disabled narrowly in
42	  that package's `analysis_options.yaml` with the reason as a comment.
43	- **Sandboxed/CI runners**: `flutter test` can stall for minutes at teardown on GPU-less containers
44	  with dropped sockets. The pattern that holds: stream output, kill the process group the moment
45	  the definitive marker prints (`All tests passed!` / `Some tests failed`), watchdog-kill on output
46	  silence. On healthy machines plain `flutter test` is equivalent — keep the wrapper thin.
47

1	---
2	name: flutter-golden-tests
3	description: Widget-test and golden mechanics in Flutter — loading real fonts before a golden, fixed-duration pumps instead of pumpAndSettle around spinners, one fixed viewport per suite. Use when writing or debugging a widget test or golden, or when goldens render as boxes, hang, or drift.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - "**/*_test.dart"
7	    - "**/test/**/*.dart"
8	---
9	
10	# Flutter widget tests and goldens
11	
12	- **Load real fonts before any golden** — the test binding defaults to the glyph-less Ahem stub
13	  (text renders as boxes). Parse `FontManifest.json` from the root bundle and `FontLoader` every
14	  family (strip the `packages/<pkg>/` prefix so plain family names resolve), which also loads
15	  MaterialIcons; bundle text faces (e.g. Roboto) in the test package's pubspec. Watch for styles
16	  that don't inherit the theme's family — `ButtonStyle`/`styleFrom` text styles are the classic
17	  leak; pin `fontFamily` there explicitly.
18	
19	- **Never `pumpAndSettle` around indeterminate progress indicators** — they schedule frames
20	  forever and the call never returns. Use fixed-duration pumps (`pump()` then
21	  `pump(Duration(...))`); this also makes an in-flight state (a spinner mid-send) a deterministic,
22	  golden-capturable frame. Corollary: after `tap()`, pump **twice** — one frame applies state, the
23	  fixed-duration pump advances implicit animations (ink ripples, color lerps) past the capture.
24	
25	- **Fix the viewport per suite**: set `tester.view.physicalSize` and `devicePixelRatio` to one
26	  phone-shaped size (and reset in teardown) so layout — and therefore goldens — can't drift with
27	  the harness default.
28

1	---
2	name: flutter-pubspec
3	description: Telling a real dependency change from lockfile churn in a Flutter app — a pubspec.lock that moved without pubspec.yaml is SDK version skew to revert, not a change to commit. Use when pubspec.lock shows up in a diff, or when editing pubspec.yaml or pubspec.lock.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - "**/pubspec.yaml"
7	    - "**/pubspec.lock"
8	---
9	
10	# pubspec and the lockfile
11	
12	- **`pubspec.lock` moving without `pubspec.yaml` moving is version skew, not a dependency change.**
13	  An app commits its lockfile (only a *library* package gitignores it), so the file is tracked on
14	  purpose — the thing to keep out of the diff is the churn a local `flutter pub get` produces when
15	  the installed SDK resolves differently from CI's. Unless you deliberately ran an upgrade, revert
16	  it: `git checkout -- pubspec.lock`.
17

1	# Python
2	
3	- **Wrapping a heavy backend behind an interface** — ship a stdlib-only implementation of that same
4	  interface for the test suite and any offline mode, and select between them at runtime through a
5	  `load_default()`/registry that lazy-imports only the chosen one, so the wiring module imports
6	  neither at load time.
7	
8	- **Importing a module only to probe whether an optional stack is present** — its name is never
9	  used, so the linter's unused-import (`F401`) is a false positive: mark the line `# noqa: F401`
10	  and record the deliberate suppression rather than deleting the probe or letting the warning ride.

15	
16	Declare heavy/native packages under `[project.optional-dependencies]`, wire the selected backend behind a tiny interface, and keep a stdlib-only implementation for the tests and offline modes.
17	
18	## Declaring the extra
19	
20	- **Adding a heavy, native or ML dependency to a Python package** — declare it under a named
21	  `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra, never in base `dependencies`: the core (logic, storage,
22	  CLI, any web layer) must import, run and be fully testable on a bare `pip install <pkg>` with the
23	  standard library alone.

1	# Static website
2	
3	- **A published file is a file the publish set names — adding a page is two edits.** The Pages artifact is assembled from `.github/site.config`'s `publish_paths` and nothing else, so a new page, stylesheet or data file that isn't under a published path (or named in the list) is simply absent from the live site, with no error anywhere: the build is green, the deploy succeeds, the page 404s. When you add a file the site serves, put it under an already-published directory or add it to `publish_paths` in the same change. The list is additive on purpose — the alternative, "publish the repo minus what we remember to exclude", publishes every draft, note and key nobody thought to hide.
4	- **The version moves with the change.** A change touching the published site raises `<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` in the same PR — `node .github/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs $(version_files)` computes it from the previous version and the UTC date, and `sw/version-bumped` is what holds the line. Never hand-write the `ymmdd` or the counter: a typed value either collides with a released one or is dated in the future, and the next bump refuses. The release flow writes no version of its own — it ships what it finds on `main` — so a shipped change without a bump is never released at all. The one deliberate human part is the **major**, a "this is a new generation of the site" statement; the owner's **"bump version"** means exactly that, and the release workflow's `bump: major` dispatch is what performs it.
5	- **The site is served from a subpath, not a domain root.** GitHub Pages serves it at `https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/` (unless a custom domain is configured), so a root-relative URL — `/style.css`, `/img/logo.png`, a `fetch('/data.json')` — resolves above the site and 404s in production while working fine in a local `file://` or `python -m http.server` preview. Write links, asset paths and fetches **relative** to the page.
6	- **Freshness is a published manifest's job, not a per-file TTL's.** There is no server here to vary `Cache-Control` per file, so the freshness policy moves into the client — and the shape it reaches for first, giving each file a lifetime matching how fast you think it changes, reprices the same bet on every file and gets it wrong in both directions at once: too long and visitors read stale data, too short and they re-download what never changed. Publish one small manifest naming every downloadable asset and a hash of its contents, fetch *that* on each load, and evict exactly the entries whose hash moved. It buys longer caching **and** fresher data, which no TTL can offer together, and the extra request is the one you are probably already making for a version string. Expect a mismatch mid-deploy — the manifest is fetched, a deploy lands, the asset that follows disagrees — so refetch once and carry on; only a disagreement that survives fresh copies of both is a fault worth surfacing.
7	- **Nothing can attest to its own freshness, and size attests to nothing at all.** A stale file carries a perfectly valid hash *of itself*, and an internal `"version"` field states which generation it is, never whether that generation is still current — so the expected hash has to come from a file fetched fresher than the one being judged, which is what makes the manifest the one asset that may never carry a TTL of its own. Caching it saves no round-trip; it moves the staleness up a level and hides it better. Nor is length a cheap stand-in for a hash: a correction applied uniformly across a file is routinely byte-length-neutral — a timezone fix rewriting every `16:25` to `17:25` moved **0 bytes** of a 3.1 MB catalogue while changing the meaning of every record in it. And record the manifest's hash beside the entry as you write it, so the check is a string compare; re-hashing the stored body means pushing megabytes through a digest on the critical path of every load to answer a question the bookkeeping already knows.
8	- **Two files cached on separate clocks and later joined *will* be joined across generations — make them a verified set or don't split them.** Splitting a payload so each half caches on its own schedule is a sound instinct and it has this cost: every visitor eventually holds one half from Tuesday and the other from Thursday. Content-addressed keys ("name the row by its date and time, not its position in the array") survive rows being *added and removed*, which is what they are usually chosen for, and not a systematic *correction to the key itself* — a timezone shift, a rounding change, a rename — which moves every key at once and joins the two halves to nothing. Have each half record the generation of the other and refetch both on a mismatch. Then assert on the join *rate*, because a partial join is silent by construction: a missing key returns "no data for this row", which is indistinguishable from a row that genuinely has none yet, and a check written as "at least one row joined" passes at 6%.
9	- **Don't call missing data survivable until you have followed it to the pixel.** "The fetch is allowed to fail — it'll just show as unknown, which we already handle" is a claim about every consumer downstream, and it is usually wrong: an absent value reaching a boolean, a comparison or a status lookup is very often indistinguishable from a real negative, so the page renders a confident falsehood with nothing logged and the visitor acts on it. Trace the missing value all the way to what it draws before deciding a failure is tolerable. Where it isn't, the file is required — fail the load and show the error state, because a wrong answer with no error is worse than an error.
10

2	name: static-site-releases

9	
10	# Releasing a static site
11	
12	Every static-site repo of ours ships the **same** pipeline: same workflows, same versioning, same
13	publish-set rules, same CI gate — so set a new repo up against that contract rather than authoring its
14	pipeline, and turn on by hand only the GitHub settings the automation cannot.
15	
16	The workflow **logic** is authored once, in this pack's [`stubs/`](../../stubs/) — the
17	[orchestrator](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-release.yml), three `workflow_call`-only **reusable
18	workflows** ([publish](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-publish.yml),
19	[deploy](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-deploy-pages.yml),
20	[bump](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-bump-version.yml)), the
21	[CI gate](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml), and three composite actions
22	([read-site-config](../../stubs/actions/read-site-config/action.yml),
23	[bump-site-version](../../stubs/actions/bump-site-version/action.yml),
24	[assemble-site](../../stubs/actions/assemble-site/action.yml)) — and **vendored into each site repo's own
25	`.github/`**, where the whole pipeline runs with no cross-repo dependency. GitHub resolves a
26	reusable workflow or a composite action only from a repo's own `.github/`, never from the shared
27	mount, so "the logic lives in the pack" means the pack holds the templates and each repo hosts a
28	*managed* copy: edit the pack, not the copy. Everything repo-specific is the keys of
29	`.github/site.config`, so every vendored file is copy-verbatim across repos.
30	
31	## The contract
32	
33	### Versioning — `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>`
34	
35	The site's version is **date-anchored**, and it is computed, never typed. The scheme, and the code
36	that computes it, live together in [bump.mjs](../../stubs/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs):
37	
38	| Part | What it is |
39	|---|---|
40	| `major` | the wrap counter. Raised by hand only as a deliberate "new generation of the site" statement — and automatically on the decade wrap (below). |
41	| `ymmdd` | the **last digit of the UTC year**, then `MM`, then `DD`. 2026-12-31 → `61231`; 2027-01-01 → `70101`. |
42	| `n` | the day's release counter: `1` for the day's first release, the previous release's `n + 1` for each further release the **same** day. |
43	
44	**Why the year digit.** The bare `MMDD` form is not monotonic across a year boundary: December
45	31st's `1.1231.3` sorts *above* the next day's `1.0101.1`, so "later" stopped meaning "bigger" —
46	which is the one thing every reader of a version assumes. Prefixing the year digit restores it:
47	`1.61231.3` → `1.70101.1`.
48	
49	**The decade wrap.** One year digit means 2029-12-31 (`91231`) is followed by 2030-01-01 (`00101`)
50	— the one legitimate decrease. The major absorbs it: `1.91231.4` → `2.00101.1`, and the ordering
51	holds forever. Any *other* decrease (a version dated in the future — a hand edit, a wrong clock) is
52	an error and fails the bump loudly; burning a major to paper over it would hide a real problem.
53	
54	**The bump belongs to the change, not to the pipeline.** A change that touches the publish set
55	raises the version in the same PR — `node .github/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs $(the repo's
56	version_files)` writes every record together — and `sw/version-bumped` is what holds that line. The
57	release flow writes no version at all: it releases whatever it finds on `main`, and no-ops when that
58	version already has a release. So the number a reviewer sees on a PR is the number that ships, and a
59	published change that forgot its bump fails on the PR rather than silently never deploying. A change
60	that publishes nothing needs no bump and redeploys nothing.
61	
62	**The major is the one bump the pipeline still performs**, because it belongs to no single change:
63	dispatch **Release static site** with `bump: major` and it raises the major, pushes it, and releases
64	the result. That dispatch is what **"bump version"** means on a site repo.
65	
66	**Moving an existing site onto the scheme** is a one-line edit, once: rewrite the current version
67	in place with the year digit inserted (`1.1231.3` → `1.61231.3`). The result is strictly greater
68	than what it replaces (`61231 > 1231`), so no tag or release ordering is disturbed and no major
69	bump is needed. Every version after that is the next change's bump.
70	
71	The version lives in the files the repo names in `version_files` — the first is the source of
72	truth, the rest must agree. `sw/version-scheme` holds them to the scheme and to each other; the
73	bump validates every record before writing any, so a failure never leaves a half-bumped tree.
74	
75	### The published artifact — an explicit list
76	
77	The Pages artifact is assembled from `publish_paths` under `publish_root`, **and nothing else**.
78	The rejected alternative is subtractive — "serve the repo except `.claude/` and `.claudinite/`" —
79	and it fails in the direction that hurts: it publishes every file nobody thought to exclude, and it
80	publishes each *new* one silently, the day it lands. An additive list can only publish what the
81	repo asked for, and its failure mode (a file that doesn't appear) is visible on the site and caught
82	on the PR. Two guards make that concrete, in [assemble-site](../../stubs/actions/assemble-site/action.yml):
83	a publish path that doesn't exist fails the run, and so does an assembled site with no `index.html`
84	at its root. Both also run on every pull request, so a broken publish set never reaches `main`.
85	
86	### `.github/site.config` — five required keys, no defaults
87	
88	A dotenv file, **every required key explicit**. A default that "happens to match" a repo's
89	layout silently publishes the wrong tree the day the layout or the default changes:
90	
91	| Key | What it is |
92	|---|---|
93	| `publish_root` | the directory the site is rooted at; `.` = the repo root. It becomes the site's `/`. |
94	| `publish_paths` | the publish set: space-separated files/directories under `publish_root`. |
95	| `version_files` | space-separated version records; the first is the source of truth. |
96	| `build_command` | what produces the publish set; `""` = nothing to build, stated. |
97	| `test_command` | the repo's gate; `""` = no tests, stated. |
98	
99	A command that needs dependencies installs them itself (`npm ci && npm test`) — that's why there is
100	no "setup" key and no assumption that a lockfile exists.
101	
102	#### `build_vars` — the one optional key
103	
104	`build_command` otherwise runs with no access to any repo configuration at all, which leaves a site
105	needing a build-time value (an analytics token, a base URL, a feature flag) with nowhere to put it.
106	`build_vars` is the declaration that closes that gap: space-separated names of **repo variables**,
107	exported into the build's environment before `build_command` runs.
108	
109	```dotenv
110	build_command=node tools/build.mjs
111	build_vars=SITE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN SITE_BASE_URL
112	```
113	
114	Three properties are load-bearing, and each is the opposite of a nearby easier choice:
115	
116	- **Optional, unlike the five.** The explicitness rule exists to stop a default from publishing the
117	  *wrong tree*; an absent `build_vars` can't do that — it means the build sees no variables, exactly
118	  what every site did before the key existed. So an untouched config keeps its exact meaning and no
119	  existing repo has to be migrated to stay valid.
120	- **A declared-but-unset variable fails the run.** Exporting an empty string instead would give the
121	  original failure one level down: the build succeeds, the page ships, and the feature that needed
122	  the value is silently dead on the live site. Better a failed deploy naming the variable.
123	- **Variables, never secrets.** The exporter is handed `toJSON(vars)`, a context that structurally
124	  cannot carry a secret — so a value that must not appear in a published artifact cannot reach the
125	  step that produces one. That boundary is a property of what the workflow passes, not a convention
126	  to remember. A build that genuinely needs a secret is doing something a published static site
127	  should not be doing.
128	
129	Declaring `build_vars` also holds the repo to a vendored copy new enough to honour it: `sw/release-workflows`
130	fails if the config names variables while the vendored action or workflows predate the exporter, since
131	that combination reads the key, ignores it, and builds with the variables unset.
132	
133	```dotenv
134	# A hand-authored site with no build step.
135	publish_root=.
136	publish_paths=index.html about.html assets data
137	version_files=package.json
138	build_command=
139	test_command=npm ci && npm test
140	```
141	
142	`read-site-config` fails the run on a missing file, a missing or empty required key, or an unknown
143	(typo'd) key; `sw/site-config` fails the same cases in the repo's own checks, plus a publish path
144	that matches nothing tracked, a tooling directory in the publish set, and a site with no
145	`index.html`.
146	
147	### The workflows
148	
149	**One orchestrator per repo** — [`static-site-release.yml`](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-release.yml),
150	named exactly `Release static site`. It owns only the triggers (push to `main`, plus a
151	`workflow_dispatch` with `force`) and calls the local publish reusable, which runs:
152	
153	| Stage | What it does |
154	|---|---|
155	| `check` | is a release due? The version on `main` has no release of its own yet — or `force`. Asking the **release list** for the current version (rather than diffing files against a tag) is what makes the flow idempotent: a failed run retries on the next push with nothing to undo, and a push carrying an already-released version is a clean no-op. |
156	| `verify` | the repo's `test_command`, on the tree being released — **before** anything is tagged or deployed. |
157	| `release` | GitHub Release `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` at that tree, auto-generated notes. |
158	| `deploy` | the Pages deploy of that exact commit, from the explicit publish set. |
159	| `report-failure` | any failure above opens a fresh `workflow-failure` issue and closes earlier open ones for this workflow as duplicates, so the newest failure is the single open bug to triage. |
160	
161	The `bump: major` dispatch pushes with `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which fires no workflow — which is why the
162	orchestrator runs the release explicitly after it rather than relying on the push trigger, and why
163	the push cannot loop.
164	
165	A push carrying a version that is already released is a clean no-op: no tag, no redeploy.
166	
167	**CI** — [`static-site-ci.yml`](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml) runs on every pull request with
168	**no `paths:` filter**: the Claudinite world sweep, the repo's `test_command`, the build, and a dry
169	run of the artifact assembly. The missing path filter is deliberate — a path-filtered conformance
170	flow arms auto-merge and then never runs, so the repo's own maintenance PR waits forever.
171	
172	## Setting up a new site repo
173	
174	1. **Declare** `static-website` in `.claudinite-settings.json` and answer the pack's two adoption
175	   questions (where it's served; what's published). Re-vendor so the pack's tree lands under the
176	   shared mount.
177	2. **Vendor the pipeline** into the repo's own `.github/`: everything under
178	   [`stubs/workflows/`](../../stubs/workflows/) and [`stubs/actions/`](../../stubs/actions/). There are no
179	   tokens to replace. A repo whose site deploys somewhere **other** than Pages takes the CI stub
180	   and the versioning half only, and skips the orchestrator + the three reusables — every rule in
181	   this pack is gated on the orchestrator, so nothing here fires on it.
182	3. **Write `.github/site.config`** with all five required keys, from the adoption answers (plus
183	   `build_vars` if the build needs repo variables).
184	4. **Put the version on the scheme** — one hand edit in each `version_files` record (`1.1231.3` →
185	   `1.61231.3` for an existing site; `1.<today's ymmdd>.1` for a new one).
186	5. **Open the one-time settings issue** (below) — idempotent: search the tracker first and skip if
187	   one already exists, open or closed.
188	6. Run the world sweep; `sw/release-workflows`, `sw/site-config` and `sw/version-scheme` are the
189	   checklist for whether the wiring is complete. `sw/version-bumped` is work-scope and shows up on
190	   the first PR that touches the publish set.
191	
192	## The settings only a human can turn on
193	
194	Repository settings are not repo content: no workflow, check or agent can set them, and a pipeline
195	that silently depends on one is a pipeline that fails on its first run for a reason nobody wrote
196	down. So they are tracked as **state, in one issue in the adopting repo** — done once, then closed
197	— not as a standing file:
198	
199	```markdown
200	### One-time GitHub settings for the static-site release pipeline
201	
202	The release pipeline is vendored and green in CI, but the following are repository *settings* —
203	nothing in the repo can set them, so they are turned on by hand (Settings → …). Until they are,
204	the first release-on-push run fails and opens a `workflow-failure` issue.
205	
206	- [ ] **Pages → Build and deployment → Source = "GitHub Actions"** (not "Deploy from a branch").
207	      Without it `actions/deploy-pages` fails and nothing is served.
208	- [ ] **Actions → General → Workflow permissions = "Read and write permissions"**, so the pipeline
209	      can create the release and push a `bump: major` dispatch. (Not needed if the repo is already
210	      on read/write.)
211	- [ ] **Environments → `github-pages` → deployment branches** must allow `main` — the default
212	      "protected branches only" rule already does; check it if the repo renamed its default branch.
213	- [ ] Optional: **Pages → Custom domain**, if this site has one. Note that a custom domain moves
214	      the site from `/<repo>/` to the domain root — see the relative-URL rule in the pack's
215	      [RULES.md](../../RULES.md).
216	
217	Close this issue once the first release-on-push run has deployed successfully.
218	```
219	
220	## Routine work
221	
222	- **Ship a change**: raise the version in the same PR (it touched the publish set, so
223	  `sw/version-bumped` requires it) and merge to `main`. The site redeploys under that
224	  `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` on its own — that is the whole release procedure.
225	- **Redeploy without a content change** (a settings fix, a first deploy): run **Release static
226	  site** from its dispatch page with `force: true`. It redeploys the existing tag rather than
227	  cutting a second one.
228	- **"bump version"** on a site repo means the **major** — the deliberate "new generation" statement.
229	  Run **Release static site** with `bump: major`; it writes every `version_files` record together,
230	  pushes, and releases.
231	- **A failed release** leaves a `workflow-failure` issue with the run link. Nothing before the tag
232	  changes anything at all, and the version is already on `main` either way — so the next push (or a
233	  `force` dispatch) releases from there with nothing to unwind.
234	
235	## What the checks hold a change to
236	
237	- **The pipeline files under `.github/workflows/static-site-*` and `.github/actions/{read-site-config,bump-site-version,assemble-site}` are managed copies of the pack's `stubs/`.** Fix the pack and re-vendor; an edit to the copy is overwritten and, until it is, makes this repo's pipeline differ from every other site repo's. The repo's own values all live in `.github/site.config`, which is what the copies read.
238

1	# web-scraping — taking data from a site you don't own
2	
3	## Finding the data surface
4	
5	- **Adding a source, or deciding what to parse** — scraping rendered markup is the **last**
6	  resort. Prefer, in order: the hydration blob a server-rendered app embeds in the page, then
7	  the JSON/GraphQL endpoint a single-page app fetches its rows from, and only then the markup
8	  — where you prefer the page's self-describing metadata (JSON-LD, `og:` tags) over element
9	  positions, because metadata survives a redesign and `.results > div:nth-child(2)` does not.
10	  Finding that surface on a new site is a one-off reconnaissance job with its own procedure,
11	  the [`map-a-data-source`](skills/map-a-data-source/SKILL.md) skill.
12	
13	- **A rendered-snapshot expectation shifting after a re-record** — rendered output is **not
14	  deterministic**, so treat the shift the way you'd treat a markup change: re-review it, don't
15	  assume a regression.
16	
17	- **Learning something non-obvious by probing the service** — write it down in a reference doc
18	  beside the scripts: endpoints, auth, the field surface, the enum values. Keep it complete
19	  enough that **nothing needs to re-probe the live service to answer a question**. The
20	  expensive part of this work is the knowledge rather than the code, and re-probing is slow,
21	  rate-limited, sometimes blocked, and occasionally the thing that gets you banned.
22	
23	## Fetching
24	
25	- **Writing the fetch itself** — browser-like headers, a randomized delay between requests, and
26	  exponential backoff on retry. Route **all** outbound page/API fetching through a single
27	  module, so swapping the vendor, the proxy or the credential is one edit with one place to
28	  test.
29	
30	- **Deciding whether to retry a failed request** — retry only what can improve. A gateway or
31	  proxy failure (408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504) is worth another attempt; any other 4xx is about
32	  your request and will answer the same way forever.
33	
34	- **Porting a fetch to a language-level HTTP client** — carry the retry policy across the
35	  rewrite. `curl --retry` covers exactly that status set and the port silently drops all of it,
36	  so the first transient 500 the old command would have ridden out kills the run.
37	
38	- **Setting the retry budget** — attempts times per-attempt timeout, plus the waits, must fit
39	  inside whatever hard limit kills the process, and the backoff should be injectable so tests
40	  exercise the retry path without sleeping through it.
41	
42	- **One item in a batch failing to fetch** — record and continue. Log the reason per item and
43	  emit a report; one unfetchable item should not abandon the batch.
44	
45	- **A sandbox refusing the target host** — an agent sandbox is commonly **bot-blocked**, and its
46	  egress proxy may refuse the host outright. That refusal is policy: **do not route around it**,
47	  not with a local fetch and not with an ad-hoc workflow spun up to reach the host. Give the
48	  fetch one sanctioned home — a scheduled job or workflow on a runner, with the credential in
49	  repository secrets — and let sessions read the committed raw records instead.
50	
51	- **A fetch that works on your machine and fails from CI** — a 403/400 or a CAPTCHA wall from a
52	  runner or a sandbox is usually the *datacenter IP* being blocked, not the headers, so tuning
53	  them is wasted work. **Reaching a commercial rendering proxy** is the standard answer: a
54	  residential lane clears the IP block, and these services usually execute JavaScript too, so a
55	  single-page app records real content. Ask it to render, and give it a wait-for-selector when
56	  the content you want arrives late. A target that stays blocked even through the proxy is
57	  un-cacheable: say so and stop, rather than hunting for another route.
58	
59	- **Needing many items from a service with no list endpoint** — no bulk endpoint is not the same
60	  as no bulk request. GraphQL lets one document alias the same field many times, and many REST
61	  APIs accept a multi-id parameter. The cap is usually undocumented, so **halve a rejected batch
62	  and retry** — that keeps batch size a throughput knob and never an accuracy one.
63	
64	- **A fetch that cannot produce a page at all** — a bot wall, a dead URL, an empty render is a
65	  dead end, not a pipeline failure: mark the item for a human and **exit successfully**. Failing
66	  the run converges on the same human signal while also implying the pipeline broke, when in
67	  fact it correctly declined. The rest of the batch should still land.
68	
69	## Reading what came back
70	
71	- **Deciding whether a fetch succeeded** — a 200 is not success. An anti-bot interstitial arrives
72	  as a normal-looking 200 (or a 403/503) whose body is a challenge page, and caching it stores
73	  garbage that looks like data. Match the known markers in the first few KB and report it as a
74	  distinct failure reason.
75	
76	- **Getting an empty body back** — nothing rendered. Treat it as a failure of that fetch rather
77	  than as an empty result, and don't retry it: a successful-but-empty response will keep being
78	  successful and empty.
79	
80	- **Choosing which field to read** — prefer the authoritative status enum over the summarizing
81	  convenience boolean, which is routinely wrong: an item can report "not sold out" while its
82	  status says there is nothing left to sell. Take the enum's legal values from the service's own
83	  options endpoint rather than from what you happened to see.
84	
85	- **Filtering rows by a status** — deny-list the bad statuses, don't allow-list the good ones,
86	  and log the set actually observed. A new status then defaults to usable and shows up in your
87	  logs, instead of silently dropping rows.
88	
89	- **Reading a numeric field** — numbers may arrive as strings. Parse; don't assume the JSON type.
90	
91	- **Reducing a set to its "cheapest" or "first"** — that value can be a special case rather than
92	  a value. Filter to what the field means before you reduce over it: a zero-priced accessibility
93	  companion band makes the cheapest ticket for every show free.
94	
95	## Normalizing what you read
96	
97	- **Converting an instant to the domain's local time** — instants usually arrive in UTC while
98	  your domain thinks in local wall-clock. Do the conversion in one function at the ingestion
99	  boundary and have everything downstream speak local time. Slicing digits out of the string
100	  files everything an hour off during daylight saving, and **the result looks completely
101	  plausible** — nothing throws, nothing is empty, the data is simply wrong. Because the failure
102	  is silent, keep a **known-answer probe**: an item whose correct value you know independently
103	  (something named after its own time, a figure published elsewhere), checked after every fresh
104	  pull. "Exactly once" cuts both ways — a stage downstream of the boundary that parses,
105	  re-offsets or re-reads a stored value as UTC is the same bug from the other end.
106	
107	- **Taking a "now"** — read it in the domain's zone rather than off the device clock. A reviewer
108	  in the same zone as the developer cannot see the difference, which is how a device clock
109	  survives review.
110	
111	- **Parsing a value whose format is ambiguous** — read it by what the page declares, centrally;
112	  never per-source, never guessed. A numeric slash date whose parts are both ≤ 12 (`05/07/2026`)
113	  has no intrinsic answer, so resolve it from a *positive* signal the document gives you (an
114	  explicit region in `<html lang>` or `og:locale`, a non-English language) and keep the default
115	  when the signal is absent or region-less, rather than inferring one from the host or the
116	  venue. Put that resolution in one helper the whole pipeline threads, so a new source cannot
117	  invent its own reading. A trailing `Z` or `+00:00` is *serialization*, not a claim about the
118	  subject's zone: it neither supplies the zone nor vetoes deriving one from what the page says
119	  about the place.
120	
121	- **Changing the conversion** — it is a **full-snapshot change**. Committed derived data is
122	  generator output, so the fix isn't done until the raw record is re-run through the new
123	  conversion and every downstream artifact regenerated. Expect the boundary to move records
124	  between partitions — items at the end of a day land in the next one, and may fall outside the
125	  range your day-partitioned files cover — and check that rather than reading it as data loss.
126	
127	- **Emitting a value your pipeline hasn't reached yet** — missing is its own state: *unknown*,
128	  never folded into *free*, *empty* or *false*. Sources keep adding rows after your last full
129	  pass, so gaps are normal and permanent. Carry unknown through the whole stack — omit the key
130	  rather than emitting a default — and let each consumer render it as its own thing.
131	
132	## What lands on disk, and when it refreshes
133	
134	- **Deciding what a fetch writes to disk** — two forms, separated deliberately. The fetched
135	  artifact (page HTML, raw response pages) is a **cache**: git-ignore it, since it is large,
136	  regenerable, and not what you reason about. The extracted raw record — the site's own object,
137	  before any of your normalization — is **committed**, and is the durable source of truth.
138	
139	- **Re-running a fetch that already ran** — **fetch only what's missing**, with an explicit flag
140	  to force a refresh, so repeat runs are a no-op. Note what "resumable" is measured against: the
141	  file on disk. On a CI runner that file is durable only once the job's commit step pushes it,
142	  so a resumable script still loses everything if the runner itself dies. Chunk the work if that
143	  matters.
144	
145	- **Scheduling the refresh** — give each field its own pass on the clock it actually moves on.
146	  The single biggest cost saving in a scraper is noticing that some fields are fixed once
147	  published, some gain rows daily and some move hourly: re-fetching everything on the fastest
148	  clock re-learns a static field nightly, thousands of requests for the same answer, and it is
149	  the part of your traffic most likely to get you blocked.
150	
151	- **Generating the artifacts downstream of the stored data** — make them a **pure function of
152	  the stored master**: refresh writes to the master, and everything else regenerates from it.
153	  Files whose inputs didn't change come back byte-identical and never enter the commit, so the
154	  diff of a scheduled run is exactly what actually moved.
155

1	---
2	name: map-a-data-source
3	description: Reconnaissance on a website you want data from but don't control — locate the real data surface (hydration blob, client API, or markup) and write the findings down before any parser exists. Use when adding a new source to a scraper, or when an existing source stops parsing and you suspect the site changed shape.
4	---
5	
6	# Map a data source before you parse it
7	
8	This runs **once per source** (and again when a site is redesigned). Its output is
9	not code — it is a committed reference doc plus one saved raw payload. Everything
10	after it is ordinary parsing.
11	
12	## 1. Fetch one page and look at what came back
13	
14	Save the raw response of a single representative page to disk and read it. You are
15	answering one question: **is the data in this document?**
16	
17	- If the interesting rows are present in the markup, you have a server-rendered page
18	  — go to step 2.
19	- If you got a small shell (a few KB of script tags and an empty root), the page is a
20	  single-page app and the data arrives separately — go to step 3.
21	
22	## 2. Look for a hydration blob first
23	
24	A server-rendered app framework almost always embeds the exact object it rendered
25	from in a script tag with a stable id. Search the saved document for a large inline
26	JSON payload and find the path to the record you want (it is usually nested a few
27	levels under a props/data wrapper).
28	
29	If one exists, **this is the surface**: it is the site's own typed record, one regex
30	and one JSON parse away, and it does not care about the layout. Save that object,
31	verbatim, as your first committed fixture.
32	
33	If there is no blob, the page's self-describing metadata (JSON-LD `<script
34	type="application/ld+json">`, `og:` meta tags) is the next-best target — it survives
35	redesigns that break element selectors.
36	
37	## 3. Find the client API
38	
39	Identify the request the page makes for its rows. Two ways in, and the second one
40	matters more than it sounds:
41	
42	- **Watch the page load** in browser devtools and read the request: URL, method,
43	  headers, auth, and the response shape.
44	- **Read the site's own JavaScript bundles.** Fetch the page, extract the script
45	  `src` paths (mind any asset prefix — the paths in the HTML already carry it),
46	  download them, and search for the operation names, query documents and field
47	  selections. For a GraphQL client the embedded query strings unescape into readable
48	  SDL, giving you the **complete** set of operations and fields the client was built
49	  against — the authoritative surface, short of introspection.
50	
51	  This path is worth knowing because it needs **only the public site host**. When the
52	  API host is blocked from where you are but the site itself loads, reading its
53	  bundle still tells you exactly what a request would look like. It cannot execute
54	  anything, so it is not a bypass of the block.
55	
56	Then note the auth story. A public listing is frequently reachable with anonymous
57	credentials the client itself ships — the same read access every visitor has. If
58	reaching the data requires a real account, stop and take that to the owner.
59	
60	## 4. Probe the shape, not just the happy path
61	
62	Before declaring the surface mapped, ask these of it explicitly, because each one has
63	silently corrupted a pipeline that assumed otherwise:
64	
65	- **Are timestamps UTC or local?** Take one item whose real-world time you can verify
66	  independently and check.
67	- **Which field is authoritative for state?** If there is both a status enum and a
68	  summarizing boolean, find an item where they disagree — there usually is one.
69	- **What are the enum's legal values?** Take them from the service's own options
70	  endpoint, not from the sample you happened to pull.
71	- **Are numbers numbers?** Amounts and counts frequently arrive as strings.
72	- **Is anything missing from this surface entirely?** A listing endpoint often
73	  carries flags but no amounts, with the real values behind a separate per-item
74	  query. Find that out now, not after you've shipped a catalogue of nulls.
75	- **Is there a bulk form?** If the per-item query has no list variant, check whether
76	  one *request* can still carry many items (GraphQL aliases, a multi-id parameter).
77	
78	## 5. Write it down, then stop
79	
80	Commit a reference doc beside the scripts holding: the endpoint(s) and auth, the
81	field surface, the enum values, each answer from step 4, and — explicitly — the
82	questions you could **not** answer and where they'd have to come from. State the
83	access constraint too: which hosts are reachable from where, and which sanctioned job
84	is allowed to do the fetching.
85	
86	The bar: **a later session should be able to write the parser from this doc without
87	touching the live service.** If it can't, the reconnaissance isn't finished.
88

1	# Executable requirements — the framework standard
2	
3	## 1. The layout is the contract
4	
5	- Everything lives under **`dev/requirements/`**: `requirements.md` (the numbered prose spec),
6	  one **top-level folder per kind**, `shared/` for cross-kind infra, and the runners/gates. The
7	  spec file's path is the framework's structural fingerprint — this pack activates on it.
8	- **The folder is the kind.** A case's kind is the directory it lives in; the case declares no
9	  kind field. Cases are
10	  `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.<ext>`: a stable feature slug (so retitling a spec section
11	  never forces renames), then the dotted leaf id.
12	- **Artifact expecteds live beside their case** (`<slug>.<id>.png`, `expected/<name>.json`);
13	  failure artifacts (actual/diff renders) go to a gitignored dir, never beside the goldens.
14	
15	## 2. The gallery is derived output
16	
17	- The spec doubles as a visual gallery: under every image-kind leaf, machine-managed image lines
18	  (tagged with an HTML comment marker) embed the committed goldens — saga leaves get their full
19	  captioned storyboard strip.
20	- A committed **gallery gate** keeps the doc equal to the generator's output byte-for-byte.
21	  Regenerate via the tool, never by hand.
22	
23	## 3. Refresh is a review step
24	
25	One committed refresh entry point regenerates all goldens **and** the gallery together, so they
26	cannot skew. Running it is how an *intended* UI change lands — the refreshed PNGs ride the diff
27	for the owner to approve. It is never how a red case gets fixed: the re-baselining approval
28	procedure (surface actual/expected/diff, ask, only then re-baseline) is canon in the
29	writing-tests skill and the spec-driven-product playbook.
30

1	# claudinite-fleet-sheepdog — the fleet enforcer marker
2	
3	## Acting on what a sweep reports
4	
5	- **Acting on an `add-packs` work-list issue** — the work is a declaration and a reviewed PR **in
6	  the named member**, never here. A session in this repo is scoped to this repo, so if every item
7	  names another repo there is nothing here to do: say the scope is the blocker rather than writing
8	  to the issues, which are the only thing within reach and are not the work.
9	
10	- **Acting on a scanned pack suggestion** — it is a recommendation, never a verdict.
11	  A fingerprint is a way to *suspect* a pack is wanted; whether to declare it is the member's call,
12	  and closing the issue `not planned` is a standing answer the scan honours rather than re-opening.
13	  A **forced** addition is the other thing entirely — a decision already made — so adopt what
14	  its issue says instead of re-judging whether it was wanted.
15	
16	- **Reading `unknown` in a report** — it means the sweep could not look, not that it looked and
17	  found nothing. Never convert one into a verdict: a repo whose declaration could not be read is
18	  neither covered nor uncovered, an undecided fingerprint is not a non-match, and a member the
19	  pack-seed sweep could not reach is not converged. Fix the access and re-run.
20	
21	- **Judging whether a member is behind** — compare `engineVersion` and `packVersions` against
22	  canon, never the age of its stamped `ref`. The update flows deliberately never rewrite `ref` or
23	  `updated`, so the stamp is provenance — which commit first vendored the mount — and stays
24	  frozen on a member that is perfectly current. Its age measures nothing, and measuring it
25	  calls the whole fleet behind on one arbitrary day.
26	
27	- **Answering why the fleet did not move** — read the member's own artifacts first: its
28	  declaration, its stamp, the runs on its head sha. This repo dispatches; each member converges
29	  itself, with its own token and its own delivery policy. Propose a settings change as a conclusion,
30	  never as the diagnosis.
31	
32	## Running the manual levers
33	
34	- **Pushing canon to the whole fleet now** — create the work item, from a checkout of this repo:
35	
36	  ```
37	  node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-tasks/queue/create-work-item.mjs claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-baseline
38	  ```
39	
40	  Add `--context "REPOS=owner/a owner/b"` to narrow it (space-separated: a Context line splits on
41	  commas), `--context "DRY_RUN=true"` to see the list without dispatching, or
42	  `--context "INCLUDE_DORMANT=true"` to reach members that stopped their own scheduler on purpose.
43	  Both knobs are read from the item's Context and nowhere else — an item created without them runs
44	  unscoped and live. It queues one run per member and then FOLLOWS each to canon's published engine
45	  and pack versions, reporting per member whether it converged, was already current, or never got
46	  there — never a count of accepted dispatches. A member with nothing to do reads `already-current`,
47	  which is a success, so over-using it is wasteful rather than unsafe.
48	
49	- **Adding a pack across the fleet** — create a `fleet-add-missing-packs` item with
50	  `--context "ADD_PACKS=…"` rather than editing anything. No pack is named anywhere in this pack's
51	  code: every id comes from config or from the item's own Context, which is what keeps the
52	  enforcer from becoming a second place packs are known.
53	
54	## Credentials
55	
56	- **Granting or repairing `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`** — a fine-grained PAT spanning the owner's
57	  repositories, granted exactly what [`fleet-token.mjs`](fleet-token.mjs)'s table names — the only
58	  place the permissions are written, because a per-sweep subset is always a defensible answer and
59	  never the right one. Grant it whole: the token is granted once, for the pack.
60	
61	- **A sweep reporting `403` or `no-permission`** — the grant is short a permission, which the
62	  error names. It is a grant to fix once, so widen the token rather than re-running: no sweep
63	  retries, because a work list nobody will act on is not a green outcome.
64

1	---
2	name: configuring-the-fleet
3	description: Editing the fleet enforcer's own config entry — the exclude list, packSeeds, and the declaration that must agree with a seed. Loaded for any edit of .claudinite-settings.json in the enforcer repo.
4	metadata:
5	  force-load-on-file-edits-paths:
6	    - ".claudinite-settings.json"
7	---
8	
9	# Configuring the fleet
10	
11	- **Keeping a repo out of the fleet** — add its full `owner/name` to `exclude` on this pack's
12	  config entry. Nothing else opts a repo out: an archived or forked repo is reported as out of scope
13	  but still walked, and a repo that simply never adopted is `uncovered`, which is a finding rather
14	  than a choice. If a repo should not be measured, say so in `exclude` and the reports stop asking
15	  about it.
16	
17	- **Adding or changing a `packSeeds` entry** — get it right *before* the sweep next runs. The
18	  sweep seeds and never overrides, so a wrong seed reaches each member exactly once and then sticks;
19	  correcting it here un-writes nothing, and undoing it is a change in every member's repo. Land the
20	  entry and its own declaration together, then read the next run's report rather than assuming.
21	
22	- **Declaring a pack this fleet also seeds** — write the same config in both places, spelling
23	  every default out on both sides rather than leaving one implicit. `seeds-agree` compares them
24	  literally, because nothing in this pack may know what one pack's absent key means. A pack the
25	  fleet standardizes on but this repo does not itself run has nothing to agree with, and is fine.
26
